Attorney General Todd Blanche later refused to rule out criminal charges against lawmakers for their investigations, as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January. Blanche later clarified his earlier remarks, saying there were "no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said."

articles.title: Perpetual paralysis: Why everything is grinding to a halt
articles.summary: From widespread airline disruptions and Microsoft's Outlook outage to the growing Nvidia scandal, America's latest failures reveal a troubling breakdown in competence, accountability and leadership.
articles.body: Doesn't anything work around here anymore? A four-hour ground stop by the FAA plunged the airline system into utter chaos, with 3,600 flights canceled, people sleeping in terminals and an absurd degree of secrecy, leaving everyone to suspect the worst. Oh sure, said Transportation chief Sean Duffy, it's just that all our crumbling equipment failed to communicate with our new equipment and this will take days to untangle. This has been a problem for years and will take $50 billion to fix. Did we forget to tell you? Two days earlier, Microsoft was so very sorry, but its Outlook email system imploded for 36 hours. Entire offices shut down because no one could get any work done, with employees unable to send messages and unaware of who was trying to reach them. OUTAGES RAISE CONCERN OVER CYBER VULNERABILITIES IN US The outages crippled governments, schools and businesses around the world. The software giant couldn't quite say what happened, first blaming its servers and then a "network capacity upgrade." But I suppose it fostered a feeling of togetherness, as if everyone was trapped in the same dark tunnel. We've all become accustomed to the frustrations of the digital world. I get 20 or more spam texts a day. I reflexively click on a button that says Stop and Delete Spam. But stopping and deleting doesn't seem to do any good, as the bogus messages keep coming in greater waves. They interrupt me again and again as a strange compulsion requires me to obliterate them. DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK We are increasingly pushed to do our business on websites because agencies and corporations don't want to spend enough money on people answering the phones. You can shout "Representative!" all you want – it's become a grim game – but still find yourself dealing with mindless bots. Embed: The thing about these websites, as you try to fill out a form or order a product, is that increasingly, many of them suck. You finish and hit "Submit" and nothing happens. You try to fill in your ZIP code but no virtual keyboard comes up. You sit through a long phone menu and hit 2, and it's not recognized — or, like a middle finger, you’re disconnected. Even Amazon has had longer delivery delays lately, making you wonder if Jeff Bezos is throwing another lavish party on some island. And if you try to book a flight online, good luck with that. If you have any complications — a minor traveling by herself, returning to a different airport than you left, attempting to get your family four seats together — you get trapped in various rabbit holes. Of course, you may have good fortune and make your reservation on a day when planes happen to be flying. And that brings me to the Huang scandal. Which at least, to its credit, has sex and espionage to entertain us while our national security is threatened. TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT Jensen Huang, one of the world's richest men, was just ousted as CEO of Nvidia, which he co-founded. The company makes advanced computer chips and is one of the most important companies on earth with one of the hardest-to-pronounce names. Huang is known for his signature black leather jackets made by Tom Ford, which go for $5,000 to $10,000 apiece. In fact, one signed by Huang was auctioned off for $960,000. Huang is giving us all a lesson in how to run a conglomerate, become a confidant of the president of the United States, and still have time for three extramarital affairs, two of them with female subordinates who report to you. Now this horndog tale would quickly fade except for the affair with the third woman, Alice Huang — the identical names making it much easier to send out invitations — who U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. And that little detail matters because we are in a fierce competition with Beijing for advanced chip supremacy. There are legal restrictions on what can be exported to Xi Jinping’s regime. And remember, Nvidia is financing the entire AI revolution. So basically, the whole world economy hangs in the balance. But no need to panic, because you can get a knockoff of one of those black leather jackets for $139. Alice Huang, a onetime television reporter, is known for her sleeveless pink dresses and sparkly heels. She was an executive at several high-tech Asian companies before becoming the controlling shareholder at Singapore-based Megaspeed. And what a coincidence, Megaspeed became a big-time buyer of Nvidia, importing billions of dollars of its sophisticated chips. She has remained totally silent. Authorities have been investigating allegations that Ms. Huang, not to be confused with Mr. Huang, has been secretly supplying China with some of these cutting-edge computer chips. While China denies this, it has a history of using female spies to lure unsuspecting execs to the boudoir – enabling the rest of us to use the tabloid phrase "honeypot scandal" without blushing. In his spare time, Jensen Huang has become a close ally of President Trump, and it probably didn’t hurt that he pledged $25 million toward the beloved ballroom. Trump, who is quite understanding about sex scandals, defended the Nvidia chief as an honorable man and called to urge him not to resign. Huang has another high-ranking supporter, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. "Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration," he says. Under Lutnick, Commerce abruptly shut down a lengthy investigation of Alice Huang’s Megaspeed and handed it off to Trump’s Justice Department. Now this is where it gets like high school. Lutnick’s arch-enemy is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; both had competed for the more prestigious Treasury job. They had a heated clash because the Treasury, Defense and State departments wanted to blacklist Megaspeed as a suspected smuggler of advanced chips to China. Now Bessent has sucker-punched his rival, taking the feud public. "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips" above a basic level, Bessent told CNBC. In the AI race, this "gives the Chinese an advantage." "Commerce had the pen," Bessent told Fox yesterday. Meanwhile, there’s been media speculation–as always!–that Huang's wife Lori knew of the romance with the suspected spy and looked the other way. The ex-CEO, who initially denied the affair with Alice Huang, later admitted it and apologized to his wife and family. At a 2021 San Jose dinner where Jensen Huang was being honored, Taiwan broadcaster TVBS examined footage of his daughter Madison, a top Nvidia executive, taking a photo of her dad and Alice Huang. The CEO can be seen putting his arm around the businesswoman's waist before leaning over to kiss her on the cheek. The two have been photographed together several times in different countries, sometimes drinking red wine, and Alice frequently posts these shots to her social media account. The Times of London says their romance was an open secret. Singapore confiscated her passport for nearly a year. MICROSOFT APOLOGIZES AFTER MAJOR OUTLOOK OUTAGE WORLDWIDE, BLAMES TECHNICAL ISSUE None of this would amount to more than a reprise of HBO's cutthroat family blood battles "Succession," were it not for the fact that the fate of our war over artificial intelligence is at stake. Huang, who is reported by Bloomberg to be "shattered," has plenty of company: top executives at HP, Intel, Microsoft, Kroger, McDonald’s, CBS and other major firms have been forced out over sexploitation activities. So let’s review. The grounding of the country's airlines, the collapse of its premier email system, the potential corruption of its massive AI investment–along with daily struggles with junk websites and overloaded phone lines–are unfolding around the same theme. America once led the world in first-rate manufacturing and superior products. And now, for all the strength of the economy, too much of this has turned sour. The CEO antics are amusing, the honeypot plots are intriguing, the Swalwell-like misconduct by resigning lawmakers is riveting, but the whole scene reeks like a towering garbage dump. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP I have a title for the inevitable Netflix series, a James Bond-style extravaganza that is probably being filmed as we speak: "Sex and the Single Spy."

articles.title: How America can win the AI race without burning voters
articles.summary: The AI industry faces a reckoning as voters backed 46 of 47 ballot measures limiting data center development over energy costs and water supply.
articles.body: One of the biggest losers on Election Day was the AI industry. Across the country, voters delivered a clear warning about the rapid expansion of data centers powering artificial intelligence. Americans want technological progress, but not at the expense of their communities, electricity bills, water supplies or quality of life. According to Ballotpedia, 46 of the 47 data-center-related ballot measures decided in 2026 favored greater limits on development. The message is unmistakable: The industry is losing public confidence, and political leaders who ignore these concerns do so at their own peril. America needs more data centers, not fewer, to maintain its AI leadership. But technology companies cannot expect communities to welcome projects when residents believe they are absorbing the costs while corporations reap the benefits. RED COUNTIES WITH DATA CENTER PROJECTS SWUNG AWAY FROM GOP IN MIDTERMS, ANALYSIS FINDS We believe there is a better way forward. In our new report, Beyond the "Wild West" and Moratorium: A Bipartisan Framework for Smart and Responsible Data Center Investment, we outline a practical approach to preserving America's AI leadership while treating host communities fairly. Our perspectives are bipartisan: Robert Wolf served as an economic adviser to President Barack Obama, while Stephen Moore served as a senior economic adviser to President Donald Trump. AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL AI is becoming one of this century's defining technologies. Data centers support cloud computing, advanced manufacturing, scientific research, national security and future AI applications. A multitrillion-dollar investment wave also creates opportunities for American workers, skilled tradespeople and domestic manufacturers. The industry has an opportunity to change course. Developers should treat residents as partners, replace vague promises with measurable commitments and pay the incremental costs their projects create. But economic benefits must be measured honestly. Construction jobs can be substantial, while permanent employment at operating facilities is often considerably smaller. Communities deserve transparency about lasting jobs, tax revenues and economic benefits. ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY: DATA Residents also have legitimate concerns about electricity demand, utility bills, water consumption, noise, traffic, pollution and lost open space. These concerns must be addressed, not dismissed. Two extremes that won't work The debate has become divided between two approaches. The first is the "Wild West": allowing development with minimal safeguards or community input. While speed matters in the global AI race, dismissing local concerns is creating the political resistance that threatens future investment. The second is the moratorium approach: pausing or halting construction until stronger regulations are established. Although the concerns are understandable, broad freezes risk delaying investment and innovation without addressing underlying problems. FROM NEW YORK TO TEXAS, STATES SHOULD RESPECT LOCAL CONTROL ON DATA CENTERS The backlash is growing. New York has pursued pauses on certain data center approvals, California has enacted oversight laws, and Texas has increased scrutiny of the industry's demands on its electric grid. Public opinion reflects these concerns. Pew Research Center found that the share of Americans who believe data centers are mostly bad for the environment increased from 39% in January to 54% in August 2026. The share believing they are mostly bad for home energy costs rose from 38% to 50%. NEIGHBORHOOD BACKLASH COLLIDES WITH AMERICA'S TECH ARMS RACE — BUT IS THIS THE PLAN TO FIX IT? A September Fabrizio, Lee & Associates survey found that nearly 65% opposed new data center construction, while 61% supported construction with conditions. Americans are not necessarily rejecting development. They are demanding reasonable protections. A bipartisan path forward The choice between unchecked development and blanket moratoriums is false. America needs predictable rules that protect consumers and communities while allowing responsible investment. Our report proposes five principles: 1. Protect electricity customers. Data center developers should pay the full incremental costs of the generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure their projects require. Residential customers and small businesses should not subsidize investments primarily serving technology companies. The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House 417–3, demonstrates support for this principle: Those driving new electricity demand should pay their fair share. 2. Protect grid reliability. Developers should disclose projected electricity demand and demonstrate how projects will affect grid reliability. Plans should address new generation, dedicated energy resources and storage without shifting costs or risks onto existing customers. 3. Safeguard water and the environment. Communities should have access to assessments of water availability, cooling requirements, emissions, noise and environmental impacts before projects are approved. Monitoring and mitigation should protect local resources and residents. 4. Require transparency and community engagement. Residents deserve early notice and meaningful opportunities to participate before major decisions are made. Developers should disclose projected jobs, tax revenues, public incentives, electricity demand and water consumption. Public incentives should be tied to measurable commitments, with reviews to ensure companies deliver on their promises. 5. Preserve local flexibility and accountability. The federal government should establish baseline protections while allowing states and localities to adapt requirements to local circumstances. Communities should retain meaningful control over siting and land use, while predictable permitting standards provide developers with investment certainty. The goal is not to dictate where every data center belongs. It is to establish clear rules for responsible development. The opportunity in the backlash There is a difference between opposing artificial intelligence and opposing how its infrastructure is being developed. Election results should not be interpreted as a rejection of innovation, but as a demand that technological progress benefit ordinary Americans. The industry has an opportunity to change course. Developers should treat residents as partners, replace vague promises with measurable commitments and pay the incremental costs their projects create. This is not an argument for less innovation. It is an argument for sustainable innovation. America cannot afford to fall behind in artificial intelligence. But the industry cannot afford to lose the public support needed to build the infrastructure AI requires. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION A responsible, bipartisan framework can protect ratepayers, respect communities, provide certainty for developers and keep America competitive. Election Day delivered a warning. The question now is whether the AI industry listens—or continues down a path of growing delays, moratoriums and political resistance. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The future of American AI leadership may depend on getting this right. Stephen Moore is a former senior economic adviser to President Donald Trump and chairman of Unleash Prosperity.

articles.title: Democrats plot massive spending spree after midterm rout — and Trump could help them pull it off
articles.summary: After their resounding Election Night victory, Democrats plot massive Medicaid restoration, ACA tax credits expansion and housing assistance funding.
articles.body: With a resounding Election Night victory behind them, Democrats are getting to work by plotting a massive government spending expansion paired with tax adjustments to pay for it. In this quest, they may find an unlikely ally in the White House. Though the new crop of Democrats doesn’t take office until early next year, many are already announcing plans to aggressively increase government healthcare expenditures, cut checks directly to voters, restore housing assistance funding and pressure the federal government into repealing cuts to the bureaucracy. Republicans, increasingly abandoning their once dogmatic opposition to increased social spending, could end up backing some of the measures Democrats seek to enact in their efforts to make life more affordable. President Donald Trump, for instance, expressed interest in cutting deals with liberal lawmakers on Election Night as it became apparent that the midterms were going to be disastrous for the GOP. Trump and Vice President JD Vance, seen by many as the president's heir apparent, have made it clear that they do not categorically oppose the extension of Affordable Care Act subsidies, one of the marquee items on the Democratic agenda, but signaled that they would like to see increased verification requirements to crack down on alleged fraud. Both have also signaled an openness to raising taxes on high-earners to help the federal government balance its budget, though estimates regarding how much these new levies would raise generally fall short of the costs that would be incurred if Democrats succeed in actualizing their demands. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS When approached by Fox News Digital, the White House kept the door open for compromise with the Democrats, so long as they don't go too far in their proposals. "President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years and a stock market that has hit record-highs," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital. "As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people," she continued. Even with sizable Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the party lacks the numbers necessary to override a presidential veto, meaning that liberals will need to work with either congressional Republicans or the White House if they want to enact key portions of their agenda. "Republicans did not lose seats because of healthcare," Michael Cannon, the Cato Institute’s director of health policy studies, told Fox News Digital when asked about whether the president should compromise with Democrats by reinstating the subsidies. "Republicans did not lose seats because they let the Obamacare subsidies for the wealthy expire, because that's what those were. When we talk about enhanced subsidies, we're talking about subsidies for people making up to $600,000 per year. That's what Democrats put in place. That's what the president rightly let expire. That's not why Republicans lost seats and, so, the president should not be afraid of standing up to the industry." TRUMP HANDING 1 MILLION AMERICANS OBAMACARE REFUND CHECKS IN 30 STATES The massive proposed spending hikes, if they are successful, would take place as the United States’ annual deficit continues to grow, reaching nearly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, while the government faces down a looming financial disaster as Social Security's retirement trust fund approaches depletion and Congress confronts difficult choices over taxes and benefits. Simply paying the interest on America’s debt cost the federal government over $1 trillion during the 2026 fiscal year. Cannon argued that, if the government spends at unsustainable levels over a long enough time period, eventually bond markets will react negatively, reducing the supply of credit and forcing the government to make steep spending cuts, as has happened in Greece and under fiscally irresponsible nations. Some on the left, however, maintain that no such shock would occur as the wealthy can simply be taxed more to reduce the need for borrowing. Though money is tight in Washington, Democrats have not pared back their spending ambitions. The crown jewel of the Democratic spending agenda is healthcare, specifically restoring Medicaid funding and Affordable Care Act subsidies. "During the first 100 days, House Democrats must act to reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote in a manifesto published Nov. 4. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the healthcare cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would reduce federal Medicaid spending by about $1.2 trillion between 2026 and 2035 at the cost of cutting enrollment in the program by about 13 million during that roughly 10-year period. As of publication, approximately 65.7 million people are enrolled in Medicaid. Republicans, especially the president, may be reluctant to work with Democrats to repeal parts of the OBBA, given the sheer amount of political capital they burned to get the bill across the finish line. The extension or expansion of ACA tax credits, however, may be more fertile ground for a bipartisan agreement. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE Trump, for instance, said in November 2025 that he would "rather not" extend enhanced ACA tax credits, but conceded that "some kind of extension may be necessary," signaling that he is at least willing to use the subsidies as a bargaining chip during negotiations. Vance, meanwhile, has stated that the subsidies "go to some people deservedly," but argued that they lend themselves to fraud while teasing a healthcare agreement he said would please both parties. Extending the enhanced ACA subsidies would come with a hefty price tag. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that making the expanded tax credits permanent would add roughly $350 billion to federal deficits between 2026 and 2035, while helping approximately 3.8 million more Americans obtain health insurance in 2035. The annual impact on the federal deficit would also climb over time, from about $23 billion in 2026 to nearly $44 billion in 2035. And because CBO's estimate only covers a 10-year period, the government would face additional costs beyond that window if the subsidies remained in place. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Some healthcare experts argue that the federal government's spending is only part of the picture. They contend that pouring more money into insurance subsidies without addressing the underlying cost of medical care can also drive up healthcare prices, potentially leaving taxpayers and consumers paying more over time. "If you want to know why healthcare is so expensive in the United States, why we spend more than any other country, why prices are higher, look at what Democrats are doing right now," Cannon told Fox News Digital. "Government subsidies drive up prices, they drive up healthcare spending ... the most inefficient healthcare sector in the world is using Democrats in particular, but Republicans too, I don't want to be unfair ... to get the government to keep pumping more and more money into that health sector." Economists generally hold that subsidizing demand for a good by providing subsidies, without increasing the supply of that good, will lead to increased costs across the market. Proponents of expanded government healthcare often counter that any reductions in efficiency or increases to costs, if such things really occur, are worth enduring to ensure coverage is more equitably distributed. Progressive Democrats led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Terri Sewell have pushed Jeffries to expand Medicare to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, set aside funds for medical debt relief and restore funding to the National Institutes of Health — proposals that could cost billions more. Some Democratic leaders have major spending proposals extending beyond healthcare. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, seen by many as a top contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, released a policy document following Election Night outlining roughly 200 policy proposals that he would like to see from the newly elected Congress. Among them are restoring government jobs at the Departments of Health and Human Services and Education, increased spending on infrastructure projects, pouring money into housing assistance programs and shoring up food assistance funding, among other priorities. PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST Jeffries and his congressional allies, meanwhile, also highlighted restoring SNAP funding, providing more government resources to cover childcare costs and subsidizing housing expenses. Some economists have argued that, by subsidizing demand for certain goods without stimulating increased supply, the government can inadvertently raise the cost of goods for everyone. On the Democratic caucus's left-wing flank, independent Sen. Bernie Sanders argued that Democrats must use their resounding victory to demand a $12,000 payment to each working-class family of four, free tuition at public universities, universal free childcare, making Medicare available to 55-year-olds, increasing Social Security benefits by $2,400 a year and boosting teacher pay. While unlikely to make its way through Congress, Sanders’ agenda would cost trillions. "The Democratic Socialists want to go much further, with universal healthcare alone, which would cost between $40 trillion and $70 trillion — roughly $300,000 to $500,000 per household," Rachel Greszler, a senior research fellow at Advancing American Freedom, a think tank affiliated with former Vice President Mike Pence, told Fox News Digital. "The entire socialist agenda calls for an estimated $71 trillion to $212 trillion in new spending over the next decade — that’s between $500,000 and $1,600,000 for every household in the US." 'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES Paying for all of this without running up the national debt too much is also on the minds of Democrats, and represents another area where they may find common ground with the GOP. Sen. Ron Wyden has floated taxing the unrealized gains of some billionaires; Democratic leadership has proposed increasing the corporate income tax; many Democratic senators have argued that additional taxes should be levied against those they deem to be high earners, and some have stated that taxes should be imposed on fast-growing sectors of the economy, such as data centers. While many of these tax hikes will likely be off the table for Republicans, Trump, Vance and a handful of congressional Republicans have expressed openness to taking more money from highly productive members of society. Vance, per reports, indicated that he would have been open to a higher tax rate for people earning more than $1 million during internal White House discussions in 2025, though the vice president has publicly expressed skepticism that taxing wealthy Americans alone could solve the country’s fiscal problems. Trump, meanwhile, has said that he would be "OK" with taxing higher earners more to assist lower- and middle-income workers — a proposal that roughly matches the Democratic policy agenda. Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Mark Kelly have proposed exactly that through their Working Americans' Tax Cut Act, which would cap the effective tax rate for most Americans while introducing a series of surtaxes on those making over $1 million per year. The University of Pennsylvania, home to one of the best business schools in the world, estimated that the proposal would net the federal government roughly $264 billion over a decade, which is not enough to cover the extension of ACA subsidies. The University of Pennsylvania's model did not take into account economic feedback effects, meaning that potential lost revenue from reduced investment or work was not captured in its estimate. Republican Sens. Bernie Moreno and Josh Hawley have backed increased taxes on high earners to pay for Social Security extensions and Child Tax Credit expansion, respectively. Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican from Maryland, has also expressed openness to a higher rate or a new bracket for million-dollar earners. Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren, meanwhile, recently introduced a bill that would raise the tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%, which analysts at the Tax Foundation and the University of Pennsylvania predict would raise either $242 billion or $300 billion, respectively, over 10 years. Combined with the millionaire tax proposal, it would generate enough revenue to offset extended ACA subsidies but would not come close to generating enough revenue to match the costs of expanding Medicaid. U.S. DEBT BLOWS PAST $40 TRILLION, JEOPARDIZING QUALITY OF LIFE FOR EVERY AMERICAN Wealth tax proposals from the Democrats' left-wing flank, while projected to raise far more in revenue for the government, have proven to be politically toxic and have drawn the ire of economists for potentially crippling economic growth. A near-term tax hike, however, may not be necessary if all the Democratic talk of healthcare funding is simply political posturing, something Cannon views as likely. "This is all kabuki here. This is not real health reform that we're talking about. All that Democrats apparently have to offer is more spending, more spending at a time when they know that existing levels of government spending on healthcare are not popular with voters," he said, pointing to the fact that voters failed to approve a billionaire tax in California to fund state healthcare. "Democrats are offering only one idea, and they know that it won't fly, but they're going through the motions because they think they can get a political advantage by saying that Republicans don't care about people." Lofty Democratic spending ambitions are not limited to the federal government. With state legislatures and governors’ mansions across the country falling into Democratic hands, public expenditures are likely to boom. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, for instance, pledged on the campaign trail to tap $17 billion from the state's rainy day fund to send $1,500 checks to every Texas household, a proposal that would require legislative approval and has since been introduced in the state Senate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While Republicans may be eager to slam Hinojosa for pulling cash from Texas’ reserves to send payments to voters, they will be forced to grapple with the fact that Trump promised to do the same, but on a much larger scale, if the GOP came out on top during the midterms.

articles.title: A blue wave, Trump’s Iran demands and a leadership fight are rattling shutdown talks
articles.summary: This month’s stunning election results have rattled the debate over government funding just weeks ahead of a shutdown deadline. Democrats are newly emboldened after a midterm rout, and some are now demanding specific provisions — like the end of the Iran war — as part of the funding package. Republicans, clashing over the cause of…
articles.body:
This month’s stunning election results have rattled the debate over government funding just weeks ahead of a shutdown deadline.

Democrats are newly emboldened after a midterm rout, and some are now demanding specific provisions — like the end of the Iran war — as part of the funding package.

Republicans, clashing over the cause of their collapse, are pointing fingers over who’s to blame and decidedly at odds over a lame-duck strategy — including their approach to government funding.

From the White House, President Trump is defying his low approval numbers by demanding hundreds of billions of dollars more for the Iran war, which was seen as a key ingredient in the electoral wins by Democrats.

In the Senate, Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) was defeated in the blue wave and is now racing against the odds to move individual spending bills as a capstone on a history-making career, even as the top Democrat on the panel is promoting a temporary stopgap package.

And across the aisle, Senate Democrats have a brand new distraction after Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched a challenge against Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to serve as majority leader next year — a surprise move that could alter the dynamics of the spending fight in the upper chamber.

The combination of factors is challenging leaders and appropriators in both parties who are scrambling to prevent a shutdown on Dec. 11. Increasingly, lawmakers think a short-term spending patch, known as a continuing resolution (CR), is the only way to do it.

“That’s where we’re headed,” said Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.).

Publicly, House Democrats insist they’re still pushing for a massive omnibus package, which would combine 12 individual bills that fund the various agencies by sector.

“We’re working to do an omnibus bill so we don’t have to do a CR,” Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) said Thursday as Congress was leaving Washington.

But while the House has passed those bills, the Senate is lagging behind. And behind closed doors, there is greater acknowledgement that the window is closing too quickly to reach an omnibus agreement between the parties and chambers.

Indeed, Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the senior Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, told Democrats at a private meeting last week that a CR is the most likely scenario, according to a senior Democratic lawmaker who was in the room.

And Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), the ranking member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, has gone a long step further, advocating publicly for a short-term CR to extend funding, at current levels, into early next year, even as Collins is still introducing separate spending bills in search of a larger omnibus.

Murray’s strategy would allow negotiators more time to hash out a deal on updated bills, but for Democrats it would also lend a clear perk: They will control both chambers in the next Congress.

“Voters handed us a huge mandate to write these bills that reflect their priorities,” Murray, who is expected to chair the Appropriations panel next year, told Politico . “So how we can lower costs and end corruption and end the war in Iran — the best way for us to do that is to do a short-term CR and then write these funding bills for next year.”

That raises the question of how long lawmakers will seek to extend current funding.

Republicans, in that debate, will likely push for a longer window, which would give them more control over funding levels next year before they lose their power in January. Democrats have different ideas, making clear that they want a short-term CR that would let them revisit the issue early next year when they control the gavels.

Asked how long a CR should be, Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), a senior appropriator, didn’t miss a beat.

“Short,” said Aguilar, who’s also in line to be the House Democratic whip next year. “I want to get, like, a real product done.”

Still, a CR of any length will pose its challenges.

Trump last week warned GOP leaders that he’s expecting them to move $350 billion in new Pentagon funding before the year’s end. He’s proposing they do it though the process known as budget reconciliation, which would allow Republicans to pass the bill without any Democratic support.

“Republicans must deliver for our Warriors. The Democrats never will,” Trump posted on Truth Social last week. “The time is NOW. MAKE AMERICA STRONG AGAIN!”

But even Republicans are warning that Trump’s strategy would almost certainly prompt Democrats to demand a $350 billion reduction in defense spending in the CR, which in turn would undermine any bipartisan spending deal and drastically heighten the odds of a shutdown.

Separately, some Senate Democrats — liberals and centrists alike — are warning that they won’t vote for any lame-duck spending package that doesn’t include specific language “that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“As we approach the December 11 funding deadline, we should not accept a short-term spending deal that continues to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice,” the senators said.

Among the senators endorsing that strategy are Sens. Michael Bennet (D), a Colorado centrist, and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), a liberal icon. Perhaps more crucially for the fate of the spending bill, the list also includes Van Hollen, who’s positioning himself as a more liberal alternative to Schumer in the race for majority leader.

Schumer says he has the support to fend off any challenge, but Van Hollen’s red lines on ending the war in the CR will only pressure Schumer to jump on board, at greater risk of a shutdown.

Democrats are also bracing for the possibility that Republicans, while they’re still in power, will try to sneak some last-minute provisions into the massive spending package and stage a vote before anyone notices.

“I don’t know if Republicans are going to want to end their rule gracefully, or whether they’re going to want to insist on controversial s— that’s going to be problematic,” said Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.).

“One of the things that I have told my colleagues is that we need to be on high alert, because these guys don’t play fair,” he added. “I mean, they try to find ways to get things over the finish line without us even knowing about it. So that’s why, whether it’s the CR or anything else, we’ve got to go through all this stuff very, very carefully.”

articles.title: Democrats mull a tricky road ahead on immigration reform
articles.summary: Democrats are exploring their options for reining in President Trump’s mass deportation operations and even undertaking immigration reform once they recapture control of Congress. But the party is split over how aggressive it can be, given the political realities of doing so while Trump remains in power. In the short term, several Democrats say they…
articles.body:
Democrats are exploring their options for reining in President Trump’s mass deportation operations and even undertaking immigration reform once they recapture control of Congress.

But the party is split over how aggressive it can be, given the political realities of doing so while Trump remains in power.

In the short term, several Democrats say they hope to use the power of the purse to claw back historic funding given to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and enact new restrictions and requirements for the agency’s officers. They also want to protect from deportation those with statuses Trump has eliminated, such as temporary protected status.

A looming question, though, is how sweeping any immigration reform can be and still win the president’s signature.

Rep. Veronica Escobar (D-Texas) publicly pleaded with colleagues Wednesday to back a bill she sponsored with Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), saying they plan to revamp and expand the Dignity Act and arguing a bipartisan bill is the only path forward.

“I am a progressive Democrat. I have very aspirational dreams and hopes for immigration reform, but I am also a pragmatist, and … as we continue to have Donald Trump in the White House, and without a supermajority in the Senate, we need Republican support. So, any comprehensive immigration reform must be bipartisan,” Escobar said, before calling on new members to help them redraft it in the coming weeks.

The bill has evolved over the years, and while it broadly provides a way for many immigrants who entered the country illegally to obtain legal status, it no longer includes a pathway to citizenship — a demand many Democrats have now that they’ve retaken Congress.

“I think it’s critical that we have a pathway to citizenship . If you take a look at what’s happened over the course of the last two years with enforcement, even people with legal status, this president has tried to take away that status. It’s only citizenship that’s going to be the protector for people who’ve been here 10, 20 years,” said Rep. Nanette Díaz Barragán (D-Calif.), a former chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

“And so that, I think, has to continue to be the benchmark for us.”

At a Wednesday press conference with the American Business Immigration Coalition and the South Texas Builders Association, advocates repeatedly urged lawmakers to bring a “fix in ’26” or “not wait til ’28” to do something on immigration reform. But the landscape is complicated.

Trump has offered mixed signals in the wake of Republicans’ bruising midterm losses.

The president has said he would be willing to work with Democrats on immigration, even calling some of his immigration policies “too tough” — such as removing those with no criminal record — but at the same time, he recently tapped Stephen Miller to serve as his chief of staff. Many Democrats describe Miller, the architect of Trump’s immigration policy, as a racist and see no real hope of working with him on the issue.

For Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), trying to gain the support of the White House feels fruitless.

“Trump’s like a very skinny palm blowing in the wind. You know, one day he’s like, ‘We were too tough on immigrants.’ The next day he’s like, ‘No amnesty.’ The next day he’s like, ‘Oh I’ll make Stephen Miller my chief of staff,’ which absolutely wipes out any possibility we’re going to do anything good on immigration. The next day he’s saying, ‘I want the Dream Act,’ you know? So, I don’t know what the guy wants,” she told The Hill, referencing a bill to protect “Dreamers,” or children who were brought to the U.S. illegally by their families.

“We need to do what we know to be right. We need to pass it in the House, in the Senate, and then send it to his bill. You never know which Trump we’re going to get. Let’s see if we can get some of these things signed.”

Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), a border-area moderate who is set to oversee the House Appropriations subcommittee on homeland security, said he’s already spoken with the White House about reining in ICE.

But he warned that Democrats could again be punished if they are too lenient on immigration — an enduring criticism of the Biden administration.

“If you want to focus on criminals, we’re with you 100 percent. But on the people that have no criminal records — as you know, there’s about 70 percent of the people that they detained have no criminal records — that’s wrong,” he told reporters of his discussions with the executive branch.

“We’re extending our hands out. If they want to work with us, we will work with them. We’re not going to be extreme. And you saw what happened with the voters … If you go extreme right, they’ll bring you back. Democrats, if we go extreme left, they’re going to come back again. So, we’ve got to make sure that we find a balanced way to address this issue.”

“Look, we have to figure out what is the best thing we can do, right? So, if we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill — I don’t know if that gets him on our side or not — then let’s do that,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said last week.

“But if that doesn’t work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either,” Gallego added.

Rep. Seth Magaziner (D-R.I.), who made headlines last year when he confronted former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem by bringing in a deported man via Zoom, said he sees the work happening in phases.

“So, I think there’s two parts. There’s sort of the short-term triage of, how do we rein in the worst abuses of the Trump administration? So, requiring all ICE agents and other DHS [Department of Homeland Security] personnel to, you know, to not wear masks, to … use appropriate force, to not separate families, not detain minors. I mean … all of these kind of short-term things to kind of put guardrails around what they’re doing,” he told The Hill.

“But then I also think that this is the time to work on a broader immigration reform policy that includes pathways to legal status for people who have been here following the laws, working for a long time, for Dreamers,” Magaziner concluded.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), set to be the incoming chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, rattled off a list of priorities — from forcing ICE to get judicial warrants to make arrests and ending their use of masks to clearing asylum backlogs to ending the practice of sending people to countries they are not from, known as third-country deportations.

“Their method of addressing immigration in this country was not who we are as a country. I don’t know what ‘look illegal’ means,” he said, arguing ICE must end racial profiling.

Others see the appropriations process as an early first step.

Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), another member of the House Appropriations Committee, said they party will look at “clawing back the money to the extent we can” by reclaiming historic funding that has not yet been spent.

Ivey said they have an avenue to do so, particularly where money was not spent as authorized, including on planes and even pro-Trump ads in the run-up to the election.

“We’ve got to try and take money back from these guys and hold them accountable that way,” he told The Hill.

Republicans, including those that have pushed for immigration reform, said they will take their cues from Trump.

“It’s also going to depend on what the president wants to do because, you know, ultimately the president is the president. The president is President Trump, and it’s going to require to see what he wants to do,” said Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart (R-Fla.), who has pressed Trump for some immigration changes and said he looks forward to “reengaging” with the White House.

Salazar took a hit within her own party by pushing the Dignity Act. She was repeatedly castigated by Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), but she appeared to take it in stride. She made criticism of Trump’s immigration agenda a centerpiece of her own reelection campaign in a district with a significant foreign-born population, narrowly winning reelection in a year many GOP colleagues did not.

“It’s up to the president. Period. It’s whatever he wants to sign. He’ll send the message to us what is he willing to do and not do. So that’s why I say he could still be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery. Now it’s up to him,” Salazar said.

But when it comes to the sweeping immigration reform so many Democrats want, there are bound to be disagreements over how far to go and with whom.

Speaking to The Hill, Escobar said she was well aware her decision to team up with Salazar irritated some colleagues.

“Even if folks get mad at me again … there’s too many people who need help,” she said.

“We can pass a Democrat-only bill in the House that goes nowhere in the Senate, and that doesn’t help anyone.”

articles.title: Trump fumes after judge blocks DC golf takeover while courses sit empty
articles.summary: President Trump is enraged at a federal judge who over the weekend put a halt to his planned redevelopment of East Potomac Golf Links, D.C.’s most popular public golf facility, while a lawsuit seeking to stop it plays out. The president has for months been preparing to take over and renovate the Hains Point…
articles.body:
President Trump is enraged at a federal judge who over the weekend put a halt to his planned redevelopment of East Potomac Golf Links, D.C.’s most popular public golf facility, while a lawsuit seeking to stop it plays out.

The president has for months been preparing to take over and renovate the Hains Point site, which is home to three golf courses, a driving range and miles of bike and jogging paths used daily by locals and tourists.

The park was set for closure on Sunday, but a temporary injunction from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes handed down just hours before the closing time put a stop to any work at the site for at least the next two weeks.

Reyes ruled the park “shall remain open and accessible to the public” except for “routine, temporary closures” that may be needed to address imminent threats to public safety.

She specifically said in her ruling the government would not be mandated to secure an operator for the golf courses, which until Sunday had been maintained by the National Links Trust, a local nonprofit dedicated to maintaining affordable golf in the nation’s capital since the coronavirus pandemic.

No tee times were available for the coming week at any of East Potomac’s three courses as of Sunday evening, and the National Links Trust did not respond to a request for comment seeking clarification on whether Reyes’s ruling had changed the organization’s plans to cede operational control of the property.

As golfers played what could be the last rounds ever teed up at the courses at East Potomac on Sunday, Trump attacked Reyes on Truth Social and echoed an argument Justice Department lawyers have made in court for weeks: Hains Point is too dangerous for the public and must be shut down.

“’Trash Island,’ as it is affectionately known, needs work, and needs it now,” Trump insisted in one post. “It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court. They don’t call it Trash Island for no reason! Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C. (and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?”

The future of East Potomac Park, which sits on National Park Service (NPS) land, has been in flux ever since the NPS terminated the trust’s lease on the property last year as Trump began making plans to erect an 18-hole, championship-style course designed by renown golf architect Tom Fazio.

The goal for the new course, Trump has said, is to construct a facility capable of hosting major professional and international tournaments.

There is widespread fear in the D.C. golf community that the new facility would price out many locals and that the course’s proposed difficulty would render it unplayable to the average amateur golfer.

Government attorneys argued in court late last week that East Potomac would become dangerous to the public with no operator at the site, and they insisted a deteriorated seawall poses a health and safety risk to the public.

Reyes pushed back on those assertions in court on Friday.

“There is no operator there because of the agency’s actions,” she said. “You don’t get to set your house on fire and then claim the insurance money. You’re the one who set the house on fire.”

Reyes has been presiding over a lawsuit that was brought against the Trump administration by a group of local conservationists and D.C. golfers who argue the president is misusing public lands to serve his personal interests.

Aside from the legal challenges it faces, major questions about the project’s feasibility and financing have lingered for weeks.

The Hains Point seawall, which has been in disrepair since 2011 and often causes major flooding issues from the Potomac River, is expected to cost hundreds of millions of dollars to repair.

The new Fazio-designed course would also require the removal of hundreds of iconic cherry trees, which bring thousands of tourists to the D.C. area each spring. Critics have questioned how downtown Washington, D.C., could handle the necessary hospitality, transportation and build-outs that would come with a major championship.

The NPS has not publicized how much the project will cost or when work there will begin, but the president has said the redevelopment will take 15 months to complete.

That’s a scenario that would leave East Potomac Golf Links closed for more than a year, and it could significantly impact the affordability and accessibility that made the facility attractive for golfers from around the region for decades.

Golfers at East Potomac have for weeks described a feeling of frustration and worry about the property’s future, given the ongoing legal challenges the project faces and a lack of comparable golfing options.

Many of them pushed back on the president’s characterization of the conditions at the current courses.

“Of course it would be good if it got a little bit nicer around here, but I don’t think the conditions are bad enough right now to justify this,” said golfer Chadwick Feeley during an interview with The Hill just before he teed off on East Potomac’s Blue Course. “I mean, I’m in a T-shirt and slip-ons right now, and I paid 28 bucks to play nine holes today … so it’s a little more relaxed and it makes it more fun and accessible for everyone.”

The president’s goal, people in both the national and local golf community contend, is to get the men’s professional game to accept one of his courses into the rotation of major championship venues.

“Trump has sought a major championship at one of his properties for his entire career in the golf business, so in everything he has said about this, it’s still clearly an obsession of his,” said Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs in the case and publisher of Beltway Golfer magazine. “It’s all about bringing a major here, which to most people that understand the golf business, course construction and how to run the logistics of something like that at East Potomac Park just seems so farfetched.”

While it is unclear when the next round of golf at East Potomac will be played, the president does not appear poised to back away from his plans to take the property over anytime soon.

“’INTERIOR’ has the absolute right to do so and will immediately appeal, on an expedited basis, this highly destructive and political decision of the judge,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!”

Friday night’s nationwide ground stop had a major impact on sporting events over the weekend. Several major college football teams and staff found their travel plans disrupted, most notably a planned game between Ole Miss and Oklahoma University, which was moved to Sunday afternoon. It was one of more than a half dozen games across the country that had their start times either delayed or postponed amid the chaos. The NFL also faced some logistical hassles in getting officials to various games around the country ahead of Sunday’s action and was forced to reassign referees in some cases.

Backers of the Protect College Sports Act are growing increasingly worried the Senate bill might not make it out of the lame-duck Congress. New York Yankees President Randy Levine, a personal friend of President Trump and leading member of his task force on college sports, penned a letter to all U.S. House members this week pleading with them to take up the legislation, writing it is the Congress’s “first post-election test” and arguing the bill is in the “9th inning, fourth quarter and final period.” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has signaled no plans to bring the bill to the floor before the end of the year.

The dangers of sports gambling and prediction markets could emerge as a hotter topic on Capitol Hill when the new Congress takes over in January. Members of both parties returned from the midterm recess expressing frustration with the sheer volume of gambling activity associated with live sports, particularly on college campuses and among younger people. Some lawmakers are vowing to place greater scrutiny on sportsbooks and prediction market platforms over what they are doing to crack down on habitual usage and harassment of athletes by bettors.

Jocks on the Hill: Rep. Blake Moore (R-Utah)

Rep. Blake Moore (R-Utah), the vice chair of the House Republican Conference, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“That’s really tough. To play, it’s always been basketball. Baseball is my favorite to be in the stadium watching, but I played college football at Utah State. But golf is all I care about now. So I don’t want to waffle. Golf is my favorite at the age of 46. That’s what my life revolves around. That and little league for my kids.”

“Oh jeez, I mean the Utes, look at us right now!”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up or one you admire currently?

“There are so many. I’m a Seahawks fan because of Brian Bosworth, but Steve Largent is the guy. I was also a Darryl Strawberry fan growing up and am still a Mets fan.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“Yeah, the Broncos. I was a Seahawks fan growing up and that was our nemesis when we were little, but we did beat them in the Super Bowl, so it’s kind of like we have a massive one up on those guys.”

“Tony Finau said the most inspirational thing I’ve ever heard an athlete say. He said Saturday night of the 2019 Masters … ‘tomorrow I’m either going to win or I’m going to learn.’ And that’s what I try to teach my boys when they play sports.”

Legendary sports broadcaster Dan Hicks died unexpectedly last week, and his New York Times/The Athletic obituary laid out his storied career calling golf, the Olympics and Notre Dame football as well as his marriage to ESPN sportscaster Hannah Storm.

The New Yorker published a deep dive into Jontay Porter, who was banned for life from the NBA for violating the league’s gambling policies and told the magazine, “we live in a generation of consumerism and greed … and I was the pinnacle of that.”

Former NFL quarterback Sam Hartman will be the next star of “The Bachelor,” ABC said late last week. Front Office Sports’s Ellyn Briggs put together a roundup of how the news was received across the world of sports and entertainment.

articles.title: Inside the Denver gathering where Democrats’ upbeat, Obama-era feel meets the 2028 race
articles.summary: Concert-style campaign posters and Obama-era energy defined the Denver gathering where Democratic leaders began jockeying for the 2028 election.
articles.body: DENVER — Live music, concert-style campaign posters and a packed schedule of Democratic leaders set the scene in Denver, where party strategists and potential 2028 contenders gathered to celebrate midterm gains and start shaping what comes next. The industrial-style venue, with indoor and outdoor spaces, gave the two-day "What’s Next" gathering a festival feel. Democrats moved between political programming, live music and social events. Beneath the party atmosphere, potential contenders tested their messages and sized up the field, as Democrats began jockeying over the party’s direction and who might lead it in 2028. The event had an unmistakably Obama-era feel, with its hopeful message and celebratory campaign atmosphere. DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE Matt Corridoni, a Democratic strategist and communications adviser at Majority Democrats, said the comparison made sense. "The theme of that campaign was hope, and a lot of folks who are here now either worked on that campaign or were inspired by that campaign," Corridoni said. "I think one of the themes of this event is hopefulness for the Democratic Party moving forward. It’s a comparison that doesn’t shock me." That hopeful energy showed up in the event’s posters and playful swag, some of which Ahmad Ali, communications director for the Searchlight Institute, helped design. DEMOCRATS RIDE MIDTERM WAVE AS 2028 HOPEFULS GATHER IN DENVER TO MAP THEIR NEXT MOVES "I think we’re seeing a Democratic Party that is younger, brighter and way more emboldened to achieve what it wants to," Ali told Fox News Digital. "So this conference, its aesthetics, whether it’s the posters you see, the fun hats, all that — it just speaks to the confidence of the era." Ali said the party’s energy could signal a break from what he described as a period of political stagnation, with voters looking for new choices in 2028. He pointed to former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign and President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory as moments that captured the political mood, while arguing that the Biden era did not carry the same cultural force. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are at the end of the Trump era, but we’re also at the end of whatever the sort of period of stuckness has plagued the Democratic Party," Ali said. "And I think that is very important, not just for Democrats, but also for all voters, because now maybe they’re going to have better options come 2028." The gathering offered a first glimpse of how Democrats hope to turn their midterm momentum into a path to 2028.

articles.title: Why Silicon Valley is backing Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang after his ouster
articles.summary: Huang’s peers, including Elon Musk, have praised his business acumen and potential risks to the US’s AI goals.
articles.body:
Some of the biggest names in the United States tech sector have launched a campaign to back former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week after reports of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Billionaire Elon Musk and several others praised Huang on social media and urged the Nvidia board to consider reinstating him. Failing to do that, they warned, could hurt US aspirations and business deals within the burgeoning artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

Huang founded Nvidia, which manufactures advanced chips used to power AI, in 1993. The company has since become one of the most valuable in the world and is a cornerstone of the US push to secure AI dominance over China.

After Huang’s resignation, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO. Since last week, Nvidia’s shares and those of some of its partners have suffered significant losses.

An online petition, meanwhile, gathered tens of thousands of signatures from Huang’s peers, former and current Nvidia employees, the company’s stakeholders and other supporters.

Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and CEO of SpaceX, has been a vocal supporter. He praised Huang’s business acumen in a post on his X platform on Saturday, arguing that Nvidia could lose business without him.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” he wrote. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, the CEOs of investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management, said Huang was an “incredible leader” and deserved a measured investigation. The firms are shareholders in Nvidia.

“Given the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure, we believe it is in the best interest of all stakeholders and certainly the shareholders of Nvidia for the Board to pursue a slow, measured and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang,” they wrote.

What is the ‘Stand with Jensen’ campaign?

Dozens of major tech leaders also signed an open letter titled “Stand With Jensen” calling for Huang’s return. They included Musk, Garry Tan, CEO of venture capital firm Y Combinator, and Steve Chen, cofounder of YouTube.

The letter, which has garnered more than 172,000 signatures, said Huang was “forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case”. It asked the board to reinstate the CEO, investigate the allegations and then publicise its findings and decisions, including how it will weigh employees’ and shareholders’ interests when taking further action.

“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter read. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the centre of this controversy was a spy.”

“Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the letter said.

Some Nvidia employees also showed solidarity with Huang who they said fostered a supportive company culture.

Darrell Dai, who identified himself as a robotics engineer, said in a LinkedIn post that he resigned in support, saying he was struggling to understand Huang’s departure “before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it”.

Huang is discussing a possible return with close confidants, according to the Financial Times.

But he faces hurdles. The US restricts Nvidia from selling chips to China, but lawmakers are now looking into whether Huang’s alleged affair may have affected the US’s own AI goals, and more seriously, whether the issue has national security implications.

At least two Congressional committees have asked Huang and senior White House officials to attend hearings in the coming weeks.

US President Donald Trump’s administration has faced criticism for allegedly failing to scrutinise Nvidia’s deals strongly enough, amid the AI race with China, with some pointing to a $25m Nvidia donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project.

The Financial Times newspaper reported that the board has already reached out to Rene Haas, CEO of British chipmaker Arm Holdings, as a potential successor. However, one of Huang’s supporters told the paper that his allies were nonetheless putting together a “war room” of tech executives to lobby for his return and were trying to gain support from the White House.

What does the scandal mean for tech founders?

The matter has rekindled a longstanding argument in Silicon Valley that founders are often unfairly treated by the very companies they founded.

Angel investor Elad Gil, who worked for Google and Twitter, said this was a good time for “founders to revisit their board” to avoid what he called a “coup”.

He cited the removal of OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman in 2023 over allegations that he was pushing profit over AI safety. Altman was reinstated a few days later after major figures such as Microsoft’s Satya Nadella offered him a position.

“Reset your board during good times to avoid sudden action during bad times,” Gil said.

Among those supporting Huang is Travis Kalanick, Uber’s cofounder and former CEO. The board asked him to resign in 2017 after allegations that he did not act on sexual harassment cases in the company. He has not returned.

Pavel Durov, founder of Telegram, warned founders not to have boards at all. In 2014, Durov was kicked off by the board of VK, his first platform, after several run-ins with Russian authorities, including for its refusal to submit protesters’ personal data to the government or to block late opposition leader Alexey Navalny from the site.

But Anthony Scaramucci, a former White House communications director and founder of investment firm SkyBridge Capital, dismissed the calls for Huang’s return.

“A suspected Chinese intelligence operative got close to the man running the most strategically important company in America,” he posted on X.

“Until every one of those probes closes, no director with a fiduciary duty can vote to bring him back. Genius doesn’t buy you an exemption from national security.”

articles.title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.summary: A number of tech figures want the board of the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.

But now fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.

The president's comments come after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.

However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report. The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

'China plays games with us, so we play games with China'

On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.

"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.

The Trump administration issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres on Monday, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models ahead of Trump's meeting with China President Xi Jingping.

The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.

The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.

The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X.

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.
