articles.title: Republicans need history lesson about their party if they want to move on from defeat
articles.summary: Jim Jordan must position himself as the imminent House speaker and drive positive solutions as the Republican Party hits a critical 2026 crossroads.
articles.body: The Republican Party is at a critically important crossroads. Understanding those crossroads and how to navigate back to a majority is a major, immediate challenge. Historically, it took Republicans a long time to recover from the Great Depression. We had become a minority party with limited appeal to over half of the country. REPUBLICANS HAVE A MIDTERM PROBLEM. REAGAN’S AMERICAN VISION IS THE ANSWER In 1980, President Ronald Reagan gave us the potential to be a truly national party for the first time since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt used the pain of the Great Depression to build massive support for the enlarged government of the New Deal and the Democratic Party that created it. In 1994, after 16 years of endless work (outlined in "March to the Majority" with Joe Gaylord, who was my partner for all those years), the Contract with America broke the Democrats’ 40-year monopoly on the U.S. House. Two years later, in 1996, the House GOP was re-elected as a majority for the first time since 1928. A genuine two-party Congress was established for the first time in two generations. NEWT GINGRICH: REPUBLICANS CAN WIN THE 2026 MIDTERMS — IF THEY FOLLOW THE PLAN Then in 2015 and 2016, then-citizen Donald Trump appealed to a wide range of hardworking people who were fed up with the corruption, left-wing extremism and dictatorial Washington bureaucracy that made their lives unhappy. By 2024, the bond between President Trump and his supporters — and their hostility to the efforts of the left to destroy him physically and legally — led the Republican Party to the edge of a genuine majority coalition for the first time since 1928. Then, at the beginning of 2025, just as we seemed on the verge of becoming a new governing majority coalition, Republicans forgot the key rules President Abraham Lincoln taught us during the GOP’s foundational period in the 1850s and 1860s. HUGH HEWITT: THE GOP IS WOUNDED, NOT DEAD — BUT RECOVERY HAS TO START NOW Lincoln warned that "with public sentiment, nothing can fail; without it nothing can succeed." He instructed us in the Gettysburg Address that we were for "government of the people, by the people, for the people." Suddenly in 2026, Republicans who had been doing a pretty good job of paying attention to the American people decided they knew more than the voters who elected them. JUSTIN HASKINS: 3 HUGE REASONS REPUBLICANS LOST. HERE’S WHAT THEY NEED TO WIN IN 2028 Republicans also reverted to a belief that enough money could drown the common sense of the American people — and that clever consultants could focus the debate and highlight selected facts, so voters would do what the consultants wanted. In some ways, the 2026 election was one of the great vindications of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Voters took back control of their country, rejected the tidal wave of advertising and political spending, and sent back a tidal wave of votes. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES Everyday folks got angry filling up their gas tanks, buying heating oil for the winter and trying to afford groceries. Then they watched a parade of billionaires who seemed to be crowding out everyday Americans who had built this country and made it an exceptional center of freedom. So, they decided to vote their anger. Lincoln warned that "with public sentiment, nothing can fail; without it nothing can succeed." He instructed us in the Gettysburg Address that we were for "government of the people, by the people, for the people." In places such as Texas, where the Republican Senate nominee may have been the most indefensible candidate in the country, people said, "Not you." They didn’t care what GOP ads said. In a shocking summary judgment, Texans not only gave Democrat James Talarico 55% of the vote, but they also wiped out every statewide Republican executive official. This was a result no one outside of Texas (and especially Washington) could have predicted. DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR In Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy ran a commercial in which his opponent’s mother attacked her. It may have been the single most self-destructive ad run anywhere in the country. It was an insult to the intelligence and decency of every Ohioan. In Mississippi, the Republican incumbent senator had said that the answer to the high price of beef was the lower cost of many other types of protein. Somehow, suggesting that Mississippians eat tofu didn’t seem to appeal to most of her voters. In some ways, it was a "let them eat cake" moment. She went from being safe in January to losing by about 6,000 votes. TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING So, Republicans need to simply make a choice. Are they going to follow the politics of Lincoln, which begins with the wishes of the American people — or the politics of money, special interests and ideologies that ignore the popular sentiment? There is a great opportunity for Republicans to see the 2026 results as a wake-up call to ask the American people what problems they want solved and what values they want defended — and then to go solve those problems and defend those values. VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS A Republican Party that’s focused on the American people will rebound with startling speed as the Democrats fail to solve practical problems and seek to impose radical values. To this end, Jim Jordan must see himself as the imminent speaker of the House and not as the incoming House minority leader. He must insist on spending two-thirds of his time on positive solutions the American people want and only one-third on what the Democrats are doing wrong. Similarly, the 2028 Republican presidential campaign should focus on what we will do better and what we will solve, not on what the Democrats are doing wrong. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION There is a deep hunger for a Lincoln-based GOP that listens to and works with the American people. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That’s where the GOP should always be — and where it should go from here. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM NEWT GINGRICH

articles.title: Historic GOP defeat fuels 11th-hour power struggle as new allies rally to rein in incoming Dem governor
articles.summary: Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison says a historic conservative coalition is demanding Greg Abbott convene a special session before Democrats take over.
articles.body: With Democrats poised to take control of the Texas governor's mansion for the first time in decades, Republican state Rep. Brian Harrison is rallying a coalition of conservative organizations behind a last-ditch push to rein in the sweeping emergency powers Gov. Greg Abbott has wielded for years. "The largest coalition of conservative organizations ever formed to restore separation of powers and rein in unconstitutional emergency powers joins the call for [Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott] to convene a special session before Democrats take over!!" Harrison wrote in a statement posted on X on Thursday. "I'm proud to be leading this effort (something I've been working on for many years on a bipartisan basis), and am grateful to [Citizens for Renewing America] for helping organize this unprecedented coalition fighting to limit the damage that Democrats can inflict on Texas if we don't act now!" he added. The announcement comes after Harrison urged Abbott on Nov. 4 to call a special session to curb gubernatorial emergency powers in the state before Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa assumes office. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI "In her first national TV appearance after winning, Gina Hinojosa agreed with me that these powers can be abused," Harrison told Fox News Digital on Friday. "I renew my invitation for her to join my call to limit them immediately, as she’s told me she wants to for years." "I will not sit silently and let Democrats turn Texas into a sanctuary state or enact socialist price controls without fighting back," the Texas Republican added. "I’m proud to provide the type of bold, pro-liberty leadership Texans deserve and honored to partner with an overwhelming and historic number of conservatives unifying in the call for action. Republicans are still in charge for months. Voters soundly rejected do-nothing Republicans, and any elected Republican advocating inaction is derelict in their duty to protect Texas." Hinojosa told MS NOW in a Nov. 5 interview that "there's no question Greg Abbott has used his emergency powers in a way that is abusive." "He has delivered a billion dollars in no-bid contracts to his donors," Hinojosa said. "My commitment is that I will only use emergency powers to deliver to the people of Texas at a time when Texans want relief, and I would hope no legislator would block that effort towards relief." Hinojosa's campaign and Abbott's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Harrison said the "growing" list of groups supporting his calls for a special legislative session includes True Texas Project, Citizens for Renewing America, Texas Gun Rights and Gun Owners of America, among several others. Citizens for Renewing America, Texas Gun Rights and Gun Owners of America each did not respond to Fox News Digital's request seeking comment. "True Texas Project has supported the call to rein in the governor's emergency powers since COVID, when Gov Abbott used extremely poor judgment in shutting our state down and stealing individual liberties," True Texas Project CEO Julie McCarty told Fox News Digital on Friday. "Now here we are at the 11th hour, scrambling to do what should have been done years ago." "Folks are saying it's too late, it can't be done, and it would be a waste of money to try," McCarty added. "They aren't wrong. So yes, we support the effort, but we're also aware it will not happen. It's simply another failure that falls at Abbott's feet and gives a perfect example why so few could get behind his re-election campaign." Harrison asserted Friday in a social media post that "this is what actual conservative UNITY looks like!" TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES Republican Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul wrote in a Nov. 8 X post that he agrees "completely" with Harrison's call for a special legislative session to rein in gubernatorial emergency powers. "Texas GOP should eliminate governor’s emergency powers," Paul said in the post. Republican Texas state Rep. Wes Virdell recently told Nexstar that calling a lame-duck special legislative session would be a "guaranteed failure" if Democrats failed to show up, potentially leaving the House short of the 100 members required to conduct business under the Texas Constitution. "It is one thing to pursue this if there was even a small chance of victory, but in my opinion this is guaranteed failure," Virdell told Nexstar in a statement. "This reminds me of running straight [into] a wall at full speed with no helmet and hoping for success. If Brian can produce a list of 15 or more Democrats that will show up so we can have [a] quorum, then count me in." Harrison acknowledged on Nov. 12 that no other state lawmakers had joined his coalition yet, but noted that Republican Texas Rep. Chip Roy and Paul had expressed support for the effort, Texas Scorecard reported. TEXAS DEMOCRATS PUT DEI BACK ON AGENDA AFTER SWEEPING TO POWER Texas' governor has the ability to sign or veto bills passed by the state's Legislature, serve as commander in chief of the state's military forces and convene special sessions "for specific purposes," per Abbott's office. Hinojosa vowed on the campaign trail that she plans to declare "a high-cost emergency" in Texas and issue executive orders to suspend the state's gas and diesel taxes and freeze residential electricity rates, the Texas Tribune reported on Nov. 4, though legal experts have questioned whether the governor has the authority to impose such a freeze. TEXAS SENATE VICTOR JAMES TALARICO LAYS OUT COMMON GROUND WITH TRUMP, VOWS TO 'WORK TOGETHER' "Greg Abbott needs to use his emergency powers to suspend the state gas tax," she wrote in an April 24, 2026, X post. "While working Texans are struggling to afford the basics, he can give immediate relief." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hinojosa is poised to take office in January 2027. Abbott has not yet announced plans to call a special legislative session before Hinojosa assumes office.

articles.title: Trump tangles with reporter on beautifying White House: ‘You’re so pathetic’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump fired back at reporters over White House renovations and denied responsibility for the FAA's first full nationwide ground stop since 9/11.
articles.body: President Donald Trump beat back questions from reporters Monday morning suggesting he was spending too much time on making improvements to the White House while the Federal Aviation Administration struggled with remaking its outdated communication systems. "You're so pathetic," Trump told a reporter when asked about the management of his time. "I have a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape," Trump said, noting he spends "very little time" on beautification projects. "It takes me 10 minutes a day." MONDAY TRAVEL FACES KEY TEST AS POSSIBLE CULPRIT IDENTIFIED BEHIND HISTORIC GROUND STOP As the reporter attempted to interject regarding federal funding priorities for the aviation system, Trump dismissed the cost of the White House repairs as "peanuts," asserting that he pays for the upgrades himself and trading personal barbs with the journalist. "This doesn’t cost money," Trump said. "This is peanuts. This is called talent. Talent. You don’t have talent, you know. You don’t know what you don’t know." When pressed later in the gaggle if he bears "responsibility" for the FAA's nationwide ground stop Friday night, the first full stoppage of flights since 9/11, Trump fired back and expressed support for Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. WHITE HOUSE SEIZES ON DELAYED OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER OPENING TO CROWN TRUMP ‘BUILDER-IN-CHIEF’ "I don't take any responsibility," Trump said. "They did a great job, Secretary Duffy. They acted incredibly. Everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing." Trump also repeated placing the blame on Congress for failing to pass the necessary funding to upgrade the FAA's telecommunications system to modernize the U.S. airline infrastructure. "I've already informed Congress, you know, we've been working with Congress to try and get the money," Trump said. "I think the one good thing that comes out of it, I'm sure Congress will now give us the money to fix [it]. "We want to have the best system in the world, and for that, we need Congress," he continued. "We've been trying to get the money for two years to fix it." "For 40 years, they should have done this with this system that's probably, on average, 50 years old," he concluded.

The president also told reporters that he did not know if Alice Huang, one of the women Jensen Huang allegedly conducted an affair with, was actually a spy, despite a U.S. intelligence assessment that she was working for Beijing. “I don’t know that she is a spy,” Trump said as he prepared to leave for his Asia trip. Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia sent ripples through the technology industry and raised questions about the sector’s vulnerabilities to Chinese espionage operations, which could have national security implications. It’s also led to volatile trading Monday in major U.S. stock indexes, of which Nvidia, worth more than $3 trillion, has formed a major component. On Monday, Nvidia shares fell more than 4% in early afternoon trading. and are down by more than 10% over the past week. Nvidia has hired an outside law firm to investigate the allegations against Jensen Huang, whose relationships may have violated company policies and who presided over export arrangements that raised concerns about Nvidia chips reaching China. Asked by a reporter what he would say to Americans who are concerned that national security was put at risk because of his close relationship with Jensen Huang and the business leader’s alleged affair with a suspected spy, Trump said that national security “was not put at risk.” Two senior U.S. officials previously told reporters they did not believe Trump would raise the Alice Huang espionage investigation with Chinese President Xi Jinping. One of the officials said Nvidia “should not really have any bearing on the trip.” Asked Monday why he was not planning to confront Xi about the alleged spying on Nvidia, Trump replied, “I may.” Trump’s openness to the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia comes as an online petition supporting the idea has garnered about 180,000 signatures. Some high-profile Silicon Valley personalities, including Elon Musk and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, said they backed the effort to restore Huang. It is not clear who is behind the petition; a message sent via a contact form to organizers was not returned. Yet the White House itself appears to be divided. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shake-up” of Nvidia’s leadership in the wake of the Huang scandal, telling Fox News that Nvidia’s board should look outside the company for its next chief executive. Bessent also suggested that other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over whether they complied with U.S. export control laws. At the Commerce Department, which sets export controls, Bessent’s national security concerns appeared to be both elevated and undermined Monday by Secretary Howard Lutnick. Elevated because the agency’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued a new chip-export rule that would close a loophole used to skirt the current export restrictions for advanced American AI semiconductors. But the agency undermined it, as well, because in announcing the rule, the Commerce Department specifically attributed the new restrictions to the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, effectively distancing itself from its own rule.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump over academic funding cuts related to DEI
articles.summary: The Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s move to abruptly cancel academic funding for researchers in California over his opposition to DEI initiatives.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald Trump’s move to abruptly cancel academic funding for researchers in California because his administration deemed the projects to be inconsistent with policies such as his opposition to DEI initiatives. The court left in place lower court rulings that said the government violated the free speech rights under the Constitution’s 1st Amendment by terminating grants issued to University of California researchers. Upon taking office in January 2025, Trump issued several executive orders telling agencies to ensure funding was consistent with his views opposing diversity, equity and inclusion programs, as well as such issues as climate change and transgender rights. At issue in the Supreme Court appeal were grants issued by the National Science Foundation and the National Endowment for the Humanities. In total, the federal government tried to end $324 million in funding to University of California institutions as part of a nationwide purge, although some funding has since resumed. Affected researchers sued, saying that the decisions discriminated against them based on their views. They alleged that the grants were cut based on keyword searches looking for words or phrases disfavored by the administration, such as “diversity” or “climate change.” Both a federal judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with the plaintiffs that the terminations violated free speech rights. But in a separate part of the case not at issue in the Supreme Court, the appeals court ruled that the plaintiffs would have to file a separate lawsuit in the Court of Federal Claims if they wanted to recoup lost funding.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects challenge to Maryland’s ‘sensitive places’ gun ban
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland’s restrictions on people carrying firearms in a broad range of public areas.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a broad challenge to Maryland’s restrictions on people carrying firearms in a broad range of public areas. The court for now sidestepped a chance to define what exactly is a “sensitive place,” a term used in previous rulings to describe locations where guns could be banned. As a result, the Maryland restrictions remain in place. The various state measures restrict carrying firearms in state parks, on public transport, on school property, in healthcare facilities and in places that sell alcohol. The court’s 6-3 conservative majority has frequently backed gun rights in a series of rulings that have expanded the scope of the Constitution’s Second Amendment, which protects the right to bear arms. Justice Clarence Thomas, part of that majority, wrote a brief statement agreeing with the court’s decision not to hear the Maryland case in part because so many distinct provisions were being challenged, saying “the breadth of petitioners’ challenge would complicate our review.” But he signaled interest in a future case that would be “more narrowly focused.” Thomas added he is “skeptical” that the various Maryland provisions are in fact lawful. The various Maryland provisions being challenged include some enacted in 2023 in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s ruling a year earlier that expanded gun rights by finding for the first time there is a right to carry a firearm outside the home. That 2022 ruling set a new test for assessing gun restrictions, putting the legal spotlight on both new and long-standing laws. When considering gun laws, judges must now focus solely on whether a law comports with a historical understanding of the Second Amendment. But in a 2008 ruling when the court first recognized an individual right to bear arms, Justice Antonin Scalia wrote in the majority opinion that “nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on ... laws forbidding the carrying of firearms in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings.” Gun rights advocates concede that there is a long history of banning firearms in certain locations, including polling places, courthouses and legislatures. But they argue that states like Maryland have gone too far in extending those bans to modern-day public places such as airports and entertainment districts. Maryland officials are “openly hostile” to gun rights, with the restrictions so broad they severely limit the ability to carry firearms in public at all, lawyers challenging the Maryland law said in court papers. They represent individual Maryland residents who want to carry guns in public as well as four gun rights groups. Other states with similarly broad restrictions include California, New York, New Jersey and Hawaii. Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, a Democrat, urged the court not to take up the case, saying in court papers that there are “vast areas of shared consensus” over which locations should be considered sensitive places. Since the 2022 Supreme Court ruling, lower courts have wrestled with how to apply the new test to modern contexts. The Supreme Court itself appeared to acknowledge that in a 2024 ruling when it upheld a federal law that prohibits people subject to domestic violence restraining orders from possessing a firearm, a decision that angered gun rights activists. In its most recent gun rights ruling, the court in June struck down a Hawaii law that sought to limit people bringing firearms onto private properties open to the public. The Maryland law contained a similar provision that was struck down by a lower court and is not at issue in the latest appeal.

articles.title: Trump's immigration olive branch threatens to open Pandora's box as experts warn of far-reaching fallout
articles.summary: Donald Trump's amnesty signal sparks fierce debate among immigration experts over rule of law, assimilation and the fiscal cost of legalization.
articles.body: After President Donald Trump signaled in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired shortly after the midterm elections that he was willing to "work on a deal" with Democrats to allow some illegal immigrants to gain legal status, Fox News Digital spoke with several immigration experts about the potential ramifications of such an agreement. The interview came just days after Republicans suffered crushing losses in the midterm elections, raising questions about whether Trump might be willing to compromise on immigration. But the president later ruled out amnesty, saying, "There won't be amnesty," while maintaining that his immigration policy had not changed. While Trump has not outlined a specific proposal, his comments have raised questions about what a potential deal could look like and how granting legal status to some illegal immigrants could impact the rule of law, assimilation and fiscal policy. TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS Fox News Digital spoke with three immigration experts about what a potential agreement could mean for the country, including its impact on the rule of law, assimilation and taxpayers. Rule of Law: "I think one of the first things we have to always consider is the impact on the rule of law and does it undermine it. It's very hard to argue that the best way to restore the rule of law and deal with illegal immigration is to reward some large fraction of people who've broken the law," said Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS). Camarota believes that amnesty begs the question of basic fairness, and impacts how people who have come to the United States legally view the immigration system. "It seems like it mocks them," he said. He used the example of a person who illegally overstays a visa to illustrate his point, saying that person shouldn't be rewarded with citizenship after overstaying a visa, especially when there are millions of people who have already followed the law and left the country when their visas expired. Laura Collins, director of immigration policy at the George W. Bush Presidential Center, acknowledged those concerns but argued that the country's immigration laws are part of the problem. AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION "I understand people's concerns about the rule of law," said Collins. "I also think you have a set of immigration laws that are not working as intended. The reason we have so many people who are here undocumented is because we have an economy that pulls in a lot of people's work, but an immigration system that restricts that labor flow." She says the United States is at a crossroads: the country can choose a system where illegal immigrants cannot stay and fix their mistakes while also contributing to the economy, or they can stay and be offered a chance at restitution. "Almost every single piece of legislation that has had a chance at passage on immigration that involves legalization program has had things like paying back taxes, going through a background check, paying some sort of fine or fee or restitution payment in order to make up for the fact that these people did something illegal by either overstaying a visa or crossing the border," she said. But Camarota questioned whether a future amnesty agreement would actually require immigrants to complete those restitution payments before obtaining citizenship. Assimilation: Camarota also said that one of the main reasons for restricting immigration in the first place is to ensure that the United States isn't overwhelmed. "We don't want the numbers to be so large that they overwhelm the assimilation process, where you can go to a school where everyone's from your background or you don't ever have to learn English, because there's enough people around you who you don't [and] who you speak your native tongue So that's one reason to limit immigration," he said. "In effect, an amnesty throws that out the window and says, well, we have these limits, but we're not going to enforce them," he continued. TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE' Drawing from the findings of a 2022 book called "Streets of Gold: America's Untold Story of Immigrant Success," Collins argued that today's immigrants are assimilating at a pace similar to that of immigrants of prior generations. America's current foreign-born population has matched a historic peak similar to late 1800s and early 1900s levels. About 15% of the current population is foreign-born. The book, she said, compared people's memories of how their grandparents and great-grandparents assimilated when they came to the United States. "And what they found was actually that immigrants are integrating it pretty much the same rates," she said. She also said that work helps people to assimilate faster, and thus, if illegal immigrants were given the opportunity to work legally, assimilation would be a smoother process. "I do think that one of the things America really is good at is us taking newcomers and turning them into Americans, and so I worry less about that" she said. "But I understand why there is a scenario where people could be afraid of that. But the data doesn't support it." Fiscal Policy: Camarota estimated that households headed by illegal immigrants receive approximately $50 billion annually in government benefits, often through programs for which their U.S.-born children are eligible. He cited Medicaid, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) and free school lunches as examples, although illegal immigrants themselves are generally barred from receiving many federal welfare benefits. TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY Illegal immigrants use welfare not because they're lazy, but because most of them do not have educations higher than 11th grade level, Camarota said. "Legalizing folks doesn't change the fact that the illegal population is overwhelmingly less educated, and less educated people just don't pay enough in taxes to cover their consumption of public services, especially when you consider all the means-tested programs they get," he said. Low-income people, he noted, simply don't pay much in taxes. "Remember, half of all workers pay no federal income tax," he said. "So, yes, illegal immigrants do pay taxes, and actually we think more than half already work on the books, so there's no big boon to taxpayers anyway. But now, they themselves will become eligible for welfare programs." Collins conceded that while many immigrants have low education levels, he said that that doesn't mean all of them are working jobs that meet their education skills. She pointed to a 2013 Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis of the Gang of Eight's immigration bill, S. 744, which estimated that the legislation would increase federal tax revenues and reduce federal deficits by approximately $158 billion over 10 years, despite increased spending on government benefits. "You get a little bit more tax revenue," she said. "They are potentially making higher wages, they're able to negotiate for different jobs and different wages because they have that legal work authorization," Collins said. HISPANIC VOTERS ARE NATURAL CONSERVATIVES. REAGAN KNEW. GOP NEEDS TO PROVE IT AGAIN She argued that with legal work authorization, some illegal immigrants would be able to fulfill their full potential in higher-level jobs. Mark Krikorian runs CIS. He said that while thinking through the pros and cons of amnesty might be a useful thought exercise, the point is probably moot. "Well, to begin with, it's not going to happen," he said of an amnesty deal. The likelihood of anything happening, certainly until the Democrats come in, until the next Congress comes in, and even then, it is, in my opinion, close to zero." For two reasons, Krikorian doesn't think Republicans have leverage to make a deal. He says Democrats won't be willing to concede any restrictions on immigration, thus leaving Republicans with no incentive to make an amnesty deal for illegal immigrants. HOUSE REPUBLICANS MOVE TO MAKE TRUMP'S BORDER POLICIES PERMANENT He used DACA as an example. Recently, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin floated the possibility of a compromise involving DACA recipients — people who came to the United States as children and received temporary protections from deportation — that could give them permanent legal status. "A DACA amnesty? Frankly, the DACAs already have amnesty. It's upgrading them from amnesty light to amnesty premium," he said. He said the first Trump administration tried making a deal for tighter immigration measures using DACA recipients as a bargaining chip. "That idea is valuable and could be productive, but there's no way that upgrading the DACA who already have Social Security numbers and work permits to regular green card status is something that the Democrats would give anything in exchange for," he said. But Krikorian warned that giving green cards to DACA recipients could eventually allow them to sponsor additional relatives, including their parents, once they become U.S. citizens, although existing immigration restrictions could prevent some relatives from obtaining legal status. "And that would have some effects, because once you have a green card, you can petition for certain relatives, and the five-year clock for citizenship starts," he said. "And when you become a citizen, you could then petition for your parents. There's no numerical caps for that." Trump discussed on "60 Minutes" potentially working out a deal that would allow some illegal immigrants working in industries like hospitality and landscaping to remain in the country. "When you go into a hotel, and you have a woman that's working there as a maid, as a cleaner as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lot of good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing," Trump said on "60 Minutes." MULLIN VOWS ‘ZERO CHANGE’ ON IMMIGRATION AFTER REPUBLICANS SUFFER CRUSHING MIDTERM LOSSES He added that people whom he described as "far-right" want deportations regardless of whether the illegal immigrant is working. The White House, meanwhile, says Trump's "strong immigration policy remains unchanged," and White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital that Democrats should work with the president to keep the border secure, remove dangerous criminal illegal immigrants from the country and stop drug trafficking. She said the president's "commonsense immigration agenda" has resulted in the "most secure border in history." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "If Democrats choose to pursue radical left open border and mass amnesty policies, they are choosing to work against the interests of the American people," she said. articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump appeal defending diversity-related grant cuts
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear an appeal by President Donald Trump's administration of a judicial decision ag...
articles.body:
FILE PHOTO: US Supreme Court building in Washington

WASHINGTON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear an appeal by President Donald Trump's administration of a judicial decision against its cuts to about $59 million in ‌federal grants to researchers in the University of California system as part of his crackdown on diversity, equity ‌and inclusion initiatives.

The Supreme Court's action means that the lower court's ruling against the administration stands and all of the grants that were cut ​off based on the perceived viewpoint of the research must continue to be restored, said Erwin Chemerinsky, a lawyer for the plaintiffs.

"I am obviously delighted that the court denied (Trump's petition for appeal)," added Chemerinsky, dean of the University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

The lower court preserved the DEI-related grants, finding that the administration's cuts likely violated the rights of the researchers under the ‌Constitution's First Amendment, which protects against government ⁠abridgment of the freedom of speech.

None of the nine justices publicly noted a dissent from the Supreme Court's action on Monday.

The cuts were part of Trump's wide-ranging actions to reshape the ⁠US government, slash federal spending and end government support for programs aimed at promoting diversity or "gender ideology" that the administration opposes.

After Trump signed executive orders in January 2025 targeting DEI and gender ideology, the National Science Foundation and National Endowment for the Humanities ​cut off ​grants for researchers in the University of California system, one ​of the world's leading public research entities.

The plaintiffs ‌filed a class-action lawsuit in 2025 on behalf of affected researchers accusing the administration of violating their First Amendment rights through discriminatory funding cuts based on the content and viewpoint of their research.

The terminated grants funded projects that included efforts to foster discussion about racial equity in science education institutions and expand science education opportunities for Indigenous youth, according to court papers.

The administration has argued that the government has broad discretion to decide what research it will fund, including the ‌ability to end financial support for projects that conflict with its policy ​agenda.

US District Judge Rita Lin halted the administration's termination of DEI-related grants, ​finding that the researchers were likely to win ​their claim that the cuts amounted to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit ‌Court of Appeals upheld that portion of Lin's ​ruling, prompting the administration's appeal ​to the Supreme Court.

The court previously allowed Trump to proceed with sweeping cuts to National Institutes of Health grants for research related to racial minorities or LGBT people, but that August 2025 ruling was based on procedural ​grounds, not the First Amendment.

The Supreme ‌Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has been highly deferential toward Trump's aggressive use of executive ​authority, vastly expanding the power of the presidency, though the justices have ruled against him in a ​few major cases.

(Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.title: Radical activist with decades-old socialist ties emerges behind Dems' under-the-radar midterm operation
articles.summary: Heather Booth, an 80-year-old socialist feminist, built the American Accountability Network's covert social media campaign that shaped midterms.
articles.body: A coordinated social media operation aimed at influencing voters ahead of the midterm elections was led in part by an 80-year-old socialist organizer who spent decades helping build the modern left's activist infrastructure, according to tax records reviewed by Fox News Digital. "The Republicans never figured out what we were doing," political commentator Van Jones said earlier this month on CNN's "The Source" with Kaitlan Collins. "There’s something called the American Accountability Network: tens of thousands of online humans, not bots, coordinated to make the affordability message a winning message online … Don’t get mad at me. I was given permission to reveal this." The American Accountability Network (AAN), which incorporation documents show was founded in early 2025, is an online activist organization that recruited both large content creators, as well as everyday Americans, and tasked them with posting, sharing and otherwise amplifying rhetoric that framed Democrats as the party of affordability — a message that exit polls suggest resonated with the electorate. Tax documents identify the woman behind the effort as Heather Booth, AAN’s president and an 80-year-old self-described "socialist feminist" who has been deeply involved in far-left activism since the anti-war movement of the Vietnam era. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE Podcaster and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino didn't buy into Jones' claims that AAN played a large part in determining the midterm elections earlier this month. "Are influencers really influencing you? Or are the influencer days numbered as people wake up to the grift. Folks, I'm leaning more towards the latter," Bongino said on the Nov. 9 episode of his show. "I don't buy any of this. ... Maybe they had some effect in certain places. My humble opinion, I don't believe it ... I'm not sure the social media ecosystem had the effect Van Jones is saying it does. I heard the same thing, the exact same argument was used to say Donald Trump stole the election through Russian Facebook ads. And that was crap, too." "Van is selling himself for the next campaign; I'm not buying it," Bongino told Fox News Digital. Booth's decades of socialist activism are documented extensively in the historical record, including in her own correspondence. In the mid-1970s, Booth and her husband were key allies of the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, a precursor to the Democratic Socialists of America, helping the fledgling organization build ties with community groups and draft a high-profile manifesto aimed at pushing the Democratic Party economically leftward, according to letters Booth wrote in 1975. Booth also disclosed in an interview that she was a founding member of the Chicago chapter of the Women’s International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell (WITCH), what she described as a "guerrilla theater" group that staged provocative protests ranging from releasing mice at a bridal fair, staging mock curses against financial institutions and using hair and nail clippings in a mock hex protesting the dismissal of a women’s liberation activist who advocated overthrowing capitalism from the University of Chicago. In a 1972 socialist feminist manifesto, Booth and her co-authors advocated for disarming police, publicly funded abortions and significant redistribution of wealth, while describing capitalism as an "institutionalized form of oppression." Booth’s late husband, whom she worked closely with throughout her career, was no less prolific or radical than she was. RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY Paul Booth is credited with authoring portions of the Port Huron statement, which framed American anti-communism as corrosive to democracy, proposed transferring certain national powers to international institutions as part of disarmament and called for greater democratic control of economic life. Booth’s husband also served as national secretary of Students for a Democratic Society, a leading New Left organization that fractured in 1969 amid ideological infighting, with one faction giving rise to the militant Weather Underground. While Heather was also an SDS member who left before the Weathermen seized control, not all of her activism was legally above board. In interviews, Booth has admitted to founding Jane, or the Abortion Counseling Service of Women’s Liberation, an organization that helped women obtain over 11,000 underground abortions before the Supreme Court mandated that the practice be legal nationwide in 1973. Law enforcement arrested seven women working for the organization in 1972 for abortion and conspiracy to commit abortion, though the charges were dropped following the court’s decision. As Jane’s operations shuttered, Booth turned to a new aim: training the next generation of activists. Booth helped establish Midwest Academy, which incorporated in 1972 and began offering general organizing training in 1973, building an institution that says it has trained more than 50,000 organizers. AAN, Jones and Booth did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital. While the individuals who lead AAN through their midterm messaging campaign are clearly disclosed in tax forms, the funding behind the effort is more opaque. Nonprofit tax disclosures operate on a roughly one-year delay, meaning that financial information is only available for its 2025 tax year, when most of its election-related activities occurred in 2026. MEMBER OF LARGEST TEACHERS UNION IN US CLAIMS ORG IS 'NO LONGER FOCUSED ON CHILDREN,' ONLY 'POLITICAL POWER' What tax documents do exist, however, begin to paint a picture of the financial forces behind AAN’s social media push. Of the roughly $280,000 AAN reported raising in 2025, $200,000 came from the American Federation of Teachers, the second-largest teachers labor union in America, according to its LM-2 disclosure. Receiving approximately 70% of its funding from a labor union during its inaugural year of operation was not AAN’s sole link to organized labor, however. Midwest Academy, where Booth still serves as chairwoman, has done considerable work training union officials over the course of its history. Union financial disclosures show that labor unions such as the National Education Association, AFL-CIO, American Federation of Teachers (AFT) and the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) have collectively pumped roughly $2 million into the organization Booth founded since 2020. Booth also directed the AFL-CIO’s healthcare campaign in 2008, helped run SEIU unionization efforts, and her late husband was a longtime American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) organizer and leader, according to her website and oral histories about her life. 'DARK MONEY’ GROUP ACCUSED OF 'SCHEME' TO TIP ELECTION IN FAVOR OF DEMOCRATS, MANIPULATE GOP VOTERS The '70s-era radical was not the only AAN leader to have ties to the labor movement. Rio Tazewell, the director of the organization, has served on working groups alongside union leadership and Reggie Hubbard, identified as a leader on incorporation documents, works with major unions on education efforts and has a board seat at a union-backed nonprofit. AAN’s public-facing website, in fact, identifies the AFL-CIO, AFT, SEIU and AFSCME as organizations it has worked with. AAN partnered with an organization called DemCastUSA, which has received $613,500 from the SEIU since 2022, to promote at least some of its social media amplification efforts. Former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones, who received significant support from organized labor during his political career, sits on DemCastUSA’s board. As AAN worked to amplify Democratic messaging across social media ahead of Election Day, Americans viewed Republicans as more politically extreme than Democrats, according to Gallup polling. The survey found that 59% of Americans considered the Republican Party too extreme, compared with 43% who said the same of Democrats. AAN’s social media boosting strategy sought to reinforce favorable perceptions of Democrats and pin Americans’ economic anxiety on GOP policies, though the polling does not establish whether the campaign influenced those views. Alongside DemCastUSA, AAN ran a program called "Amplifier Army" that aimed to give left-of-center voices a privileged slot in social media algorithms by coordinating interactions that would give such posts a larger reach. "Together, we're building a network of organizers, creators and everyday people who use their social media to flood the feed with the content and calls to action that move this fight forward — at the inflection points where public pressure actually shifts the outcome," a sign-up page for the program reads. Participants are invited to "share coordinated priority content at the moments that matter most" and "amplify calls to action from movement partners across all major platforms." FAR-LEFT GROUPS PIVOT FROM MAY DAY PROTESTS TO MOBILIZE VOTERS FOR 2026 MIDTERMS, PUSHING DEMS LEFTWARD Fox News Digital attended an Amplifier Army training session earlier in November, obtaining an audio recording, screenshots of the pitch deck shown to participants, a link to the program’s group chat and an invitation online platform used to coordinate social media engagement. The WhatsApp group chat only has around 80 members. However, during the training session, the organizer in charge mentioned that they had recently created a new chat because their original forum on Signal had reached maximum capacity. The maximum number of participants in a Signal chat is 1,000. At the end of the presentation, participants were instructed to create an account on an online app called ProSocial. The platform feeds an array of posts to users, all from mid-to-large Democratic-aligned social media accounts, and instructs users to like, comment, share, save and repost the content in question. Points are assigned for each action and the individual who gets the most points at the end of every month receives a prize from the organization. A slide included in the training session’s slide show indicated that posts with partnered accounts selected for amplification saw a double-digit increase in shares and likes relative to posts from partners held back from amplification at random. Fox News Digital was not able to independently verify this data. The organizer running the training session claimed that those behind the Amplifier Army coordinated with socialist activists in Brazil to help build their system, seeking to emulate the online push that helped Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva win an upset victory in Brazil’s recent presidential election. Despite the considerable reach AAN claims for its social media operation, questions remain about how much influence the effort actually had on the midterm elections. Increased energy costs, rising grocery bills and stubbornly high housing prices, for instance, gave Americans reasons to be dissatisfied with the administration, regardless of what they did or didn’t see on social media. Additionally, even with a thousand active members dutifully boosting posts curated by AAN, it is unclear how much of a difference that could have made on social media platforms trafficked by billions of users. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That said, AAN claims to include massive left-leaning media outlets in its network, including ​​MeidasTouch, which consistently generates hundreds of millions of monthly views and downloads.

articles.body:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have agreed to disband the department's Strategic Response Group, or SRG, after months of discussions, officials announced Monday.

"What we're doing today is announcing the disbanding of the Strategic Response Group and announcing a completely new approach to how we treat protest in our city," Mamdani told Eyewitness News in an exclusive joint interview with the NYPD Commissioner.

The SRG is the NYPD's citywide rapid-deployment force that specializes in counterterrorism but also responds to major crimes and mass demonstrations. Critics have argued that the unit's crowd-control tactics are heavy-handed and provocative.

Tisch said the SRG's 500 highly trained, uniformed officers will be reassigned, with many moving to the department's Counterterrorism Bureau.

When asked whether the move represented a compromise, Tisch said, "No, I would never compromise on security for New Yorkers. And over the past year, we have made a number of massive changes in the department that strengthen our counterterrorism efforts, this among them."

Mamdani said the city's new approach will focus on reducing tensions during demonstrations.

"In addition to separating out those responsibilities, we're also emphasizing an approach of de-escalation, an approach of dialogue," he said.

Over the next year, the city plans to hire and train civilians to work with protest organizers before and during demonstrations. Tisch said the change will not affect how the NYPD responds to civil disorder.

"Nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions, like, for example, the celebrations following the Knicks' epic championship," Tisch said. "And so New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to."

Disbanding the SRG was one of Mamdani's campaign promises. The unit is scheduled to be dissolved in the spring of next year, when a new NYPD crowd-control unit will assume responsibility for facilitating nonviolent protests.

See more of N.J. Burkett's exclusive interview on Eyewitness News First at 4:00 p.m.

Thenew strategyincludes the following measures:

Establishes a civilian-leddialogue unit:

Creates the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD)withinthe Mayor's Office of Community Safetyto plan for and respond to protestsincoordinationwith the NYPD's FAST team.

EstablishesFAST, a team of30 uniformed officers within the Community Affairs Bureauwithspecialized trainingin communication and de-escalationand coordination with crowd-management personnel. FAST will handle dialogue and de-escalation while CDDD is being built.

Establishesthe Patrol SupportDivision, which reports to the Patrol Services Bureau and will comprise vetted officers who will receive specialized training and conduct arrests at protests in rare instances, if necessary. PSD will work with CDDD and FAST when respondingtoFirstAmendment activities, building on the reforms agreed to in the Payne Protest Settlement. For the vast majority of the time, PSD will serve as a resource to patrol, including participating in searches for missing persons, supporting major events, such as the NYC Marathon and Thanksgiving Day Parade, and assisting with priority traffic posts during hazardous weather. There will be strict eligibility requirements to enter the PSD.

Regulates aggressive crowd-management tactics:

Codifies the ban on kettling, prohibits the use of long guns and tear gas during First Amendment activities and limits long-range acoustic devices to 90 decibels. Pepper spray will not be used as a general crowd-management device.

These reforms will be implemented at no additional cost and without increasing or reducing NYPD headcount.

articles.title: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson faces audit calls after CFO quits over 'financial integrity' concerns
articles.summary: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson faces fresh budget turmoil after CFO Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigns, questioning the city's financial reporting and budget calculations.
articles.body: Chicago’s chief financial officer, who formerly worked for a top credit ratings bureau, resigned Friday citing financial integrity concerns, casting a shadow over the fiscal management of progressive Mayor Brandon Johnson amid a fight over the FY-2027 budget. Chicago CFO Ashlee Gabrysch served only three months before the onetime Fitch Ratings executive stepped down, saying she could no longer meet her professional obligations under the conditions of her employment, according to a resignation letter obtained by the Chicago Tribune. "The chief financial officer’s statements about the city’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate," Gabrysch wrote, according to the Tribune. "I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve." Johnson did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment, but his press secretary accused Gabrysch of being "largely absent" during key parts of the next budget’s creation process. CHICAGO MAYOR CALLS ICE RAIDS ‘TERRORISM,’ SAYS TRUMP'S AMERICA APPEARS AS ‘IF THE CONFEDERACY WON’ The mayor's office also accused Gabrysch of improperly directing a $75 million payment to city pension funds before the required legal procedures had been completed, saying it would refer the matter to Chicago's Office of Inspector General for review. The Tribune recounted recent events in the budget process involving Gabrysch, including that she disagreed with Johnson over assertions about the size of the city’s deficit. In September, Johnson announced that the Windy City faces a projected $882 million budget shortfall in 2027, which local media described as smaller than a typical election year and lighter than the $1.15 billion deficit projected in 2025. The city holds its elections in odd years. "We have difficult and consequential decisions ahead of us as we work to address the structural financial challenges that have confronted Chicago for decades," Johnson said at the time, according to Chicago’s PBS affiliate. However, according to the Tribune, Johnson claimed the true figure is now $662 million, "adjusted" in concert with planned borrowing to help fund settlement amounts involving police officers. CHICAGO MAYOR CALLS DOGE AN ‘ACT OF WAR’ Gabrysch challenged that accounting during budget hearings, arguing that the settlement expenses should remain part of the deficit and that borrowing to pay them amounted to a temporary fix rather than a lasting solution. While the administration maintained that 76% of its budget measures addressed underlying financial problems, Gabrysch calculated the figure at just 56%, according to the Tribune. Alderman Marty Quinn, D-Midway, questioned Johnson’s handling at the time, according to the paper, saying he was "not surprised that the mayor may be a little disingenuous here, that seems to be his normal course." Gabrysch also stopped short of calling Johnson's proposed $17.6 billion budget balanced during an October City Council hearing, arguing that the city needed to demonstrate progress toward reducing future deficits, according to Crain's Chicago Business. City Comptroller Michael Belsky maintained that proposed revenues matched expenditures, while acting Budget Director Jonathan Ernst defended the administration's calculations and its plan to borrow roughly $480 million to cover legal settlements. Gabrysch warned that the city anticipated issuing $350 million in settlement-related bonds in 2027, with an estimated $190 million in interest costs over seven years, according to Crain's. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Her resignation prompted Council Finance Committee chairman Pat Dowell, D-South Loop, to call for an independent audit. The departure adds to a wave of turnover in Johnson's financial leadership, including two previous CFO departures this year and the resignation of the city's budget director in August. The upheaval comes as Chicago grapples with mounting financial obligations and credit-rating downgrades.

articles.title: Seattle mayor orders park named for American president renamed
articles.summary: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson ordered Jackson Park renamed, citing Andrew Jackson's legacy of forcibly displacing Native American peoples from their lands.
articles.body: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson has ordered a city park named after President Andrew Jackson to be renamed to better fit "the values of our city." The city argues that Jackson's legacy includes policies that forcibly displaced Native American peoples from their ancestral lands. Wilson directed the Seattle Parks and Recreation to begin a community renaming process on Monday. The 160-acre Jackson Park plays host to the Jackson Park Golf Course. "We’ve heard from community members who want to change the name of Jackson Park, and now is the right time to move this conversation forward. With new light rail connections and opportunities to make the park more accessible and welcoming, we should have a park that reflects the values of our city," Wilson said in a statement. WASHINGTON AG'S OFFICE INDICATES IT WILL DEFEND GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE AFTER ACLU SUES TO BLOCK IT "I’m directing Seattle Parks and Recreation to begin a community naming process to find a name that better reflects this place, its history, and the people who enjoy it," she added. The renaming effort comes just days after Wilson also backed an effort to block a girls sports initiative that overwhelmingly passed a statewide vote. SEATTLE MAYOR BACKS EFFORT TO BLOCK GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE THAT PASSED IN 36 OF WASHINGTON'S 39 COUNTIES Wilson said last week that she supports the Seattle School Board's unanimous vote to pursue legal action against Initiative 638 — which would enforce separation of boys and girls in K-12 sports in Washington state. Voters passed the measure by a 13-point margin last week, and it won in 36 of the Evergreen State's 39 counties. But after deliberating behind closed doors Monday, the Seattle School Board voted publicly to authorize potential legal action against the measure without hearing public testimony. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Last night, the Seattle Public Schools Board of Directors voted to authorize legal action regarding Initiative 638. The Board's decision reflects concerns shared by educators, families, community leaders, and the City of Seattle about the measure's impact on student privacy, safety, dignity, and equitable access to educational opportunities," Wilson said in a statement last week. Fox News' Matt Calkins contributed to this report.

articles.title: Poll: 35% of Trump Voters Skipped Midterms
articles.summary: Poll: 35% of Trump Voters Skipped Midterms
articles.body:
New survey results show that 35% of President Donald Trump's 2024 voters didn't cast a ballot in the midterm elections.

The findings suggest Republicans' crushing losses this month were driven largely by Trump supporters staying home rather than abandoning the GOP for Democrats, according to a new J.L. Partners analysis reported by the New York Post .

The pollster found that low Republican turnout accounted for 10 percentage points of the 15-point swing toward Democrats since 2024, while voters switching parties accounted for the remaining five points.

Just 8% of Trump's 2024 supporters voted for Democrats on Nov. 3.

"The GOP should not throw the MAGA baby out with the bathwater just yet," J.L. Partners founding director James Johnson said, the Post reported.

"If Republicans can energize their 2024 vote in 2028, then they may yet have a shot at winning again."

The analysis, based on an Election Day survey of 1,000 registered voters and more than 30,000 campaign interviews, found particularly steep turnout declines among key segments of Trump's coalition.

Among his 2024 supporters, 46% of those without college degrees failed to vote, along with 44% of those older than 65 and 39% of rural voters.

Johnson said the turnout collapse alone would have cost Republicans control of Congress, even without voters switching parties.

"Even without a single voter switching, the GOP would have lost the Senate and House," Johnson said.

The findings bolster Trump's argument that Republicans suffered because he wasn't on the ballot.

However, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis suggested GOP voters stayed home because they were dissatisfied with congressional Republicans' performance.

"A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate," DeSantis told Fox News.

The survey also found potential vulnerabilities for Democrats heading into 2028.

Nearly half of Democrat voters, 48%, said their midterm vote was primarily against Trump rather than in support of Democrat policies.

Only 30% of registered voters believed Democrats have a viable presidential candidate for 2028.

Meanwhile, CNN reported that Trump's declining popularity remains a significant obstacle for Republicans.

CNN's voter polling found that 86% of Americans who disapproved of Trump's performance backed Democrats in House races.

Cost of living emerged as the leading concern across every demographic group in the J.L. Partners survey.

Johnson suggested the Iran war contributed to voter frustration over rising prices, particularly gasoline.

The survey's overall margin of error was 3.4 percentage points.

Despite the GOP's losses, Johnson said the results indicate Republicans could rebound by rebuilding turnout among Trump's 2024 supporters rather than abandoning the political coalition that returned him to the White House.

articles.title: Fetterman's Gaza-born challenger calls to 'abolish ICE,' oust top Democratic leaders
articles.summary: Gaza-born socialist Ahmed Moor challenged one of Israel's strongest Senate supporters while calling for an overhaul of Democratic leadership.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: It’s a circumstance almost ripped from a screenplay: a Gaza-born political newcomer wants to topple one of the Senate’s staunchest supporters of Israel in the Democratic Party. But for Ahmed Moor, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who is the first to toss his hat into the arena to challenge Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., the story doesn't end there. "Look, so this race is not about John Fetterman," Moor told Fox News Digital in an interview. "John Fetterman's story is over, but the story of the United States continues. I'm getting in now because I believe we're in the midst of a constitutional crisis." GAZA-BORN DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST LAUNCHES PRIMARY BID AGAINST SEN JOHN FETTERMAN "I have some compassion for John Fetterman — I want to depersonalize," he continued. "Let's talk about policy. The policies that man has expressed and committed to are just a reflection of the special interests which have run his office for too long now. The problem of John Fetterman's policies is the problem of corruption in America." Fetterman is up for re-election in the 2028 cycle and has become a target for Democrats in Pennsylvania ready to replace him as he continuously moved more to the center of the political spectrum and aligned with Republicans on key issues like the war in Iran, government funding and immigration. Whether he runs again for a second term remains in the air. When asked by Fox News Digital if he had made a decision, Fetterman said, "The more, the merrier," to challengers entering the Democratic primary. But Moor, so far, is the only candidate officially in the race. FETTERMAN WARNS THERE IS NO LONGER 'COMMON GROUND' WITH FAR-LEFT DEMOCRATS OVER ISRAEL "I know, he seems to really love Hamas," Fetterman said. "And now, so, like, so if you tell him, say thank you for running." Moor was born in Gaza before immigrating to Philadelphia, where he went to public schools, attended the University of Pennsylvania and later went to Harvard to obtain a public policy degree. His policy positions are in line with the growing progressive flank in the Senate Democratic caucus and echo the positions that Fetterman first ran on in 2022 when he pledged to support the Senate’s progressive standard-bearer, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., if he won. "I spent a lot of time on international policy, kind of a foreign policy specialist, one of the reasons the Senate job appeals to me," Moor said. "But equally, I'm committed to what I call the ‘Dignity Agenda,’ which is universal access to healthcare, childcare and affordable housing." Among the top concerns for Moor in the "constitutional crisis" he sees in the country is freedom of speech, which he contended came under assault during the Biden administration when protests against "the genocide in Palestine" exploded across college campuses. FETTERMAN PLAYS POLITICAL MAVERICK, BUT HIS VOTING RECORD TELLS ANOTHER STORY "Students were brutalized for assembly, for speech," Moor said. "That shouldn't happen in America. Donald Trump stepped through that breach and accelerated the assault. And ICE today is the worst expression, the violation of due process in America." Like other Democrats and progressives, Moor wants to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), but he would "like to see immigration law enforced." "ICE is a lawless organization — ICE is a paramilitary militia. ICE is not law enforcement," he said. "Let's abolish ICE. Let's hold the bad actors who've killed Americans and kidnapped others in our streets. Let's hold them to account for breaking our local ordinance and our local laws. That's a criminal matter today in America. I hope local prosecutors run with it." And like other progressives who scored stunning victories during the midterm elections to help flip the Senate, like Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, Moor is against the old guard of Democratic leadership staying in charge. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It’s a position that is gaining steam in the Senate, where Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is mounting a rare challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead Democrats through the forthcoming majority in the upper chamber. Moor said Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., both have to go. "Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries don't have what it takes to meet the moment. They need to be replaced," Moor said. "This campaign is also about sustaining pressure in that direction. If they survive the leadership contest, which is underway today, I'm going to continue to sustain the pressure on both of those men to do the right thing continuously."

The Pentagon referred Fox News Digital to CENTCOM, which did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Monday. IRAN VOWS 'WE WILL FIND YOU' TO 2 US NAVY OFFICERS THE DAY WARSHIP RETURNS FROM MIDDLE EAST The news comes as the U.S.-Iran war continues more than eight months after it began earlier this year. articles.title: Trump leaves door open to Kim Jong Un joining high-stakes talks with Xi, Putin
articles.summary: Trump suggested Kim Jong Un could appear during his China trip, saying the North Korean leader's presence is up to Xi Jinping ahead of trilateral talks in China.
articles.body: President Donald Trump offered a brief, unexpected response about North Korea during a White House gaggle Monday, adding a new wrinkle to his closely watched trip to Asia this week. Trump suggested North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could make an appearance during his China trip, telling reporters, "We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come, I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi." The comment came in response to a reporter's question about the upcoming high-stakes meetings between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, and whether the trio planned to discuss North Korean nuclear capabilities. PRESIDENT TRUMP TO HOLD HISTORIC TRILATERAL SUMMIT WITH XI AND PUTIN Trump and Kim last met in 2019, when their Hanoi summit ended without an agreement on North Korea’s nuclear program. Nonetheless, Pyongyang has since expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities, while efforts to restart talks have stalled. In August, Trump said he expected to meet Kim "later this year," but North Korea pushed back, with Kim Yo Jong saying the leaders’ relationship remained "excellent" while accusing Washington of maintaining hostile policies toward Pyongyang, Fox News Digital reported at the time. Meanwhile, a U.S. official said last week, according to ABC News, that there were no plans for North Korea engagement during Trump’s Asia trip, and experts say the country is unlikely to feature prominently in the trilateral talks. South Korean news outlet Yonhap News Agency reported Monday that South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said it hoped high-level talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit would contribute to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula. South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun reportedly raised the possibility of renewed U.S.-North Korea dialogue at the summit with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in Beijing on Friday, stressing that South Korea has vital interests in Korean Peninsula issues and hopes that its perspective is taken into account. NORTH KOREA MISSILE COULD PUT GUAM IN RANGE AS KIM REBUFFS TRUMP OUTREACH: EXPERT The South Korean news agency also reported Monday that Andrew Yeo, a senior fellow at the U.S.-based Brookings Institution, said North Korea’s nuclear program is unlikely to be discussed at the summit, citing differences between Washington and Moscow over Pyongyang’s nuclear ambitions. The report also highlighted comments from Korea Economic Institute senior fellow Ellen Kim, who reportedly suggested the leaders could briefly discuss North Korea behind closed doors, but nuclear arms control and the war in Iran are likely to take priority. Ellen Kim added that Xi or Putin could relay a message from Trump to Kim Jong Un, though they may be reluctant to support U.S.-North Korea negotiations for fear of losing influence over Pyongyang. The trilateral meeting is scheduled for 2:30 p.m. Thursday local time at Shenzhen Kylin Villa, according to Trump’s public schedule. White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said Friday that Trump planned to discuss nuclear arms reduction with Xi and Putin, while a senior U.S. official said Iran would also be on the agenda. The Associated Press reported Monday that Trump plans to raise Russia’s war in Ukraine at the meeting as well.
