SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I think he's backing down a little bit. I think he could be tougher," Trump told reporters Monday outside the White House. "I think it could be a lot tougher, frankly." Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for additional comment.

articles.title: Trump brings two divided Cabinet heavyweights to China as controversy hangs over high-stakes talks
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Scott Bessent and Howard Lutnick hold opposing views on China as both join his high-stakes Asia trip to meet Xi Jinping.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is bringing two powerful Cabinet officials divided over restrictions on China's access to advanced American AI chips on his high-stakes Asia trip, as controversy over the issue follows them into talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are both accompanying Trump on the four-day trip despite reports of a dispute over whether to blacklist a company suspected of helping China obtain restricted American AI technology. Trump acknowledged their competing views Monday and suggested Lutnick may have delayed action to avoid worsening relations with Beijing. "He might have delayed it, but he was doing that because you could have if you didn't delay it. If you didn't do something, you could have a blow up with China. We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides," the president said. The dispute follows reports that Lutnick resisted efforts to place Singapore-based Megaspeed on a U.S. trade blacklist, despite Trump reportedly supporting action against the company on three occasions this year, according to Axios. Megaspeed has faced allegations that its operations helped Chinese companies gain access to restricted Nvidia chips. TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT The Commerce Department announced a new rule this week aimed at preventing Chinese companies and other restricted foreign entities from accessing advanced American computing technology through data centers in third countries. The department said the rule was written at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council. Trump told reporters Monday he is not considering replacing Lutnick, saying "he's done a very good job." Bessent publicly confirmed Friday that several administration departments had supported adding Megaspeed to the Commerce Department's Entity List, which would restrict the company's access to U.S. technology. "Treasury, War, USTR and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said. The Commerce Department denied Axios' account of a confrontation between Bessent and Lutnick in the White House Situation Room, saying the two officials had no such conversation. Trump is bringing several of his administration's most powerful officials on the four-day Asia trip, which includes stops in the Philippines and China. TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA The delegation includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Bessent, Lutnick, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, among other officials, a White House official confirmed to Fox News Digital. Trump is expected to meet with world leaders, participate in regional economic and security summits and hold high-stakes talks with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and possibly North Korea leader Kim Jong Un. The controversy has also drawn attention to Nvidia's leadership. Nvidia announced Thursday that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned following reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for China. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said Sunday that it retained outside counsel to investigate allegations surrounding its operations. Trump said Monday it has not been confirmed she is a spy. FEDERAL PROSECUTOR WARNS SEN WARREN OF 'LEGAL CONSEQUENCES' IF RECORDS AREN'T PRESERVED IN TRUMP-LINKED PROBES Lutnick, the former chairman and CEO of investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald, is one of the wealthiest officials to serve in a presidential administration. A longtime Trump ally, he co-chaired the president's 2024 transition team, and the two have known each other for decades through New York's business and social circles. Lutnick has also agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 amid growing scrutiny of the Commerce Department's handling of Nvidia chip exports to China, CBS News reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., jointly called on the administration to preserve records related to Nvidia's advanced AI chip exports and potential national security risks. The senators set a Nov. 17 deadline for written confirmation that the records would be preserved and requested a congressional briefing. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Fox News Digital reached out to the Departments of Commerce and Treasury for comment.

articles.title: Trump criticizes '60 Minutes' bosses as 'even worse' as he challenges Iran war report
articles.summary: President Donald Trump blasted CBS' "60 Minutes" for omitting U.S. defensive wins against Iranian drones in a report as he lashed out at the news program.
articles.body: President Donald Trump criticized CBS' "60 Minutes" on Monday, following correspondent Norah O’Donnell’s report on a deadly Iranian attack against American troops in Kuwait — accusing the program of omitting U.S. defensive successes. "The new people running 60 Minutes are even worse than their predecessors. A recent study on an attack in the early stages of Iran was not correctly stated," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. A CBS insider defended its investigation and pointed to reports of another Iranian drone attack targeting an American base in Bahrain. "The Truth Social post on U.S. drone capabilities (despite reports of an Iranian drone strike on another US base in Bahrain yesterday) is an attempt to distract from 60 MINUTES’ 8-month investigation that revealed U.S. military failures surrounding the deadliest attack against U.S. troops in the war with Iran," a CBS insider told Fox News Digital. TRUMP DOUBLES DOWN ON ATTACKS AGAINST 'TERRIBLE' '60 MINUTES' HOST NORAH O'DONNELL Trump's criticism centered on the program’s treatment of U.S. defenses since Operation Epic Fury began Feb. 28. He cited thousands of Iranian drone launches while defending the military’s performance. "Since February 28, 2026, the start of Epic Fury, Iran has fired between 8,000-9,000 One-way Attack Drones," Trump said on Truth Social. "Only 2 of them got through, resulting in U.S. fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia." The president also cited approximately 2,000 Iranian ballistic missiles and one that caused American fatalities in Jordan. He combined interceptions and attacks that did not cause American deaths in assessing the military's defenses. "Translation: 99.99% of Iranian missiles and drones have been shot down or, in any event, not caused U.S. deaths. CENTCOM defensive measures have been historically effective. No one in the World has the ability to do so well. All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes 'report,'" Trump said. The president's criticism of the show was noteworthy as many liberal critics have accused new CBS editor-in-chief Bari Weiss of being too Trump-friendly, despite "60 Minutes" running numerous critical segments under her watch. ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER' Sunday's "60 Minutes" report by O'Donnell was part of what the network called an eight-month investigation into the Iran war. The report says it reveals the "extent of the damage to U.S. positions in the Middle East," a well as the human costs for the loved ones of the 23 U.S. service members killed and 800 wounded in the conflict. The CBS insider's response focused on alleged decisions preceding the Kuwait strike, including warnings about the installation's vulnerability and its ability to treat wounded soldiers. "Norah O'Donnell reported that military leadership at the targeted Army post in Kuwait allegedly disregarded threats of Iran kamikaze drone attacks, ignored U.S. intelligence about Port Shuaiba being on Iran’s target list, failed to deliver a counter drone system, and lacked the basic medical capabilities, including an onsite physician," the CBS insider told Fox News Digital. "All of this leading to the vulnerability of an unprotected American base and death of 6 soldiers." The insider also directed Fox News Digital to its broadcast transcript, which described satellite imagery and video documenting damage to at least 31 American military and diplomatic sites across eight countries. COST OF IRAN WAR EXPLODES AS TOLL ON US AIR FLEET NEARLY DOUBLES The Pentagon declined to answer whether the unit received adequate protection, according to the source. That account concerned The Pentagon’s response to CBS' reporting, rather than a response to Trump’s Monday criticism. The Pentagon previously defended precautions at the installation. In a March post on X responding to CBS News' reporting about the site’s fortifications, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell disputed the characterization of the command center as a makeshift office space. articles.title: Senate takes big step toward passing permitting reform package
articles.summary: The Senate took a big step Monday to advance a bipartisan permitting reform package closer to final passage by voting to end debate on a managers’ amendment to strengthen provisions of the bill addressing energy-hungry data centers and protecting tribal sovereignty. Senators voted to invoke cloture 70-27 on the substitute amendment sponsored by Sen. Shelley…
articles.body:
The Senate took a big step Monday to advance a bipartisan permitting reform package closer to final passage by voting to end debate on a managers’ amendment to strengthen provisions of the bill addressing energy-hungry data centers and protecting tribal sovereignty.

Senators voted to invoke cloture 70-27 on the substitute amendment sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee.

The procedural vote sets up a vote on final Senate passage of the legislation before the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill would speed the construction of energy, mining and infrastructure projects while limiting environmental challenges under the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

It seeks to dramatically boost the capacity of transmission lines and could reduce the time it takes to build new lines from 10 years or longer under current law to five or six years.

It would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish timelines for utilities to upgrade their transmission lines and implement advanced technologies when benefits outweigh costs.

A significant number of Democrats voted to limit debate on the substitute amendment even though it’s not clear whether they will be able to offer additional amendments to the proposal.

Some Senate Democrats who voted to begin debate on the bill, such as Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), threatened to oppose bringing it up for a final vote unless changes were made. Cortez Masto specifically called for striking out a section of the bill affecting the National Historic Preservation Act.

The bill still needs to pass the House, where Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) has called for changes to address grid reliability.

It also faces opposition in the lower chamber from pro-conservation advocates such as Reps. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), Summer Lee (D-Pa.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.).

Huffman, who is in line to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, says the bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, would constrain National Environmental Policy Act reviews, radically alter transmission approvals and let companies sue the government for damages if they can show they were discriminated against based on fuel type.

Grijalva issued a statement last week declaring that “Congress should not be rushing to pass a bill that gives [President Trump] even more unilateral authority to bypass our laws.”

Some Democrats are concerned by Trump’s threat that he will continue to block the construction of wind turbines, even if the bill passes.

“I will not approve wind turbines,” the president vowed. “Wind turbines are a major loser.”

Several leading environmental groups oppose the legislation, including the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, and the Southern Environmental Law Center.

Industry groups such as the Data Center Coalition, the American Petroleum Institute and the National Mining Association support the legislation as do labor unions such as the AFL-CIO and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers.

The bill has strong Democratic support in the Senate thanks to the backing of Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee ranking member Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Environment and Public Works Committee Chair Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.).

Whitehouse told The Hill Monday that prospect of the bill passing the House “seems pretty good” and downplayed the criticism of some House Democrats.

“There aren’t many bills that pass around here without some criticism,” he said.

He said that the Senate floor staff is now trying to work out an agreement on amendments.

Heinrich said the legislation would ensure that data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause and would lower electricity prices for families.

He noted that the substitute amendment incorporated “feedback we’ve heard from Tribes” who were concerned that it would undermine the federal government’s obligation to consult with them on infrastructure, energy and mining projects affecting their ancestral lands.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help lower energy costs, strengthen Tribal consultation and create more good-paying jobs,” he said after introducing the substitute amendment with Capito, Whitehouse and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chairman Mike Lee (R-Utah).

The Rhodium Group estimates the bill will reduce household electricity bills by $50 to $78 a month per year by 2040 by allowing more lower-cost energy sources to reach the grid and shielding taxpayers from data-center costs.

The substitute amendment expands the list of entities that may serve as a “lead agency” to include a Tribal or state government agency with regard to a proposed project.

And it clarifies that projects financed by the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act and the Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing Programs are not excluded, among other changes.

Whitehouse, a leading Senate advocate for addressing climate change, said the bill will “juice the clean energy economy” and help Americans “build big things again,” reduce pollution and create new well-paying union jobs.

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), who is seeking to become chairman of the Senate Environment in Public Works Committee next year, opposes the legislation as does nearly half of the Senate Democratic caucus.

He said the bill “accelerates the extraction and burning of fossil fuels” and would make it “easier to build more data centers powered by ‘behind the meter’ natural gas plants,” referring to data centers and other industrial facilities that receive power directly from a natural gas plant without it touching the public utility grid.

The legislation has strong support from Trump, who is expected to sign it into law if it reaches his desk.

“We’re behind it 100 percent,” Trump told reporters last week.

Trump said he may help Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) whip House Republicans to support the legislation.

articles.body:
Air Force One was rerouted Monday over extreme weather as President Trump and administration officials head to Asia to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Due to extreme weather conditions in Anchorage, Air Force One landed in Fairbanks in order to refuel under better climate conditions,” a White House official told NewsNation, The Hill’s partner. “We have now departed for the Philippines.”

Traveling with Trump is Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and various White House staffers.

Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation. Top agenda items are expected to include AI, trade and security issues.

The U.S. and China extended their bilateral trade truce through Jan. 10 but still have much to discuss on trade, particularly, as the deal potentially lapses. The initial deal lowered U.S. tariffs on Chinese exports and saw China agree to suspend its export controls on rare metals.

The president has floated a meeting with North Korean President Kim Jong Un while in China to restart nuclear program talks. He also told reporters he would talk with Chinese and Russian leaders about the war with Ukraine despite Trump administration officials previously claiming that would be off the agenda.

“We’ll talk about, my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing Ukraine,” Trump expressed Monday. “Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers in the month. So we’ll be talking about that.”

The talks come as one of Trump’s closest allies, Jensen Huang, was ousted from major AI chip firm Nvidia over a series of extramarital affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump has backed Huang throughout the entire scandal, but Congress has already launched probes into Huang and the Commerce Department over the incident.

Senate steps toward passing permitting reform package

The Senate took a big step Monday to advance a bipartisan permitting reform package closer to final passage by voting to end debate on a managers’ amendment to strengthen provisions of the bill addressing energy-hungry data centers and protecting tribal sovereignty.

Senators voted to invoke cloture 70-27 on the substitute amendment sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the chair of the Environment and Public Works Committee.

The procedural vote sets up a vote on final Senate passage of the legislation before the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill would speed the construction of energy, mining and infrastructure projects while limiting environmental challenges under the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

It seeks to dramatically boost the capacity of transmission lines and could reduce the time it takes to build new lines from 10 years or longer under current law to five or six years.

It would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish timelines for utilities to upgrade their transmission lines and implement advanced technologies when benefits outweigh costs.

A significant number of Democrats voted to limit debate on the substitute amendment even though it’s not clear whether they will be able to offer additional amendments to the proposal.

articles.title: Vance mocks Democrats for accusing Trump of being ‘soft on China’
articles.summary: Vice President Vance mocked Democrats who accused President Trump of being “soft on China” amid criticism of the administration’s handling of the Nvidia scandal. “Now again, I find it just hysterical that the Democrats are accusing Donald Trump of being soft on China,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News. “When it comes to…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance mocked Democrats who accused President Trump of being “soft on China” amid criticism of the administration’s handling of the Nvidia scandal.

“Now again, I find it just hysterical that the Democrats are accusing Donald Trump of being soft on China,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News . “When it comes to export controls, when it comes to ensuring that American chips, the most advanced American chips, stay with American technology providers, nobody has been better on this than the Trump administration.”

“So I really think that what the Democrats are doing is they’re using a lot of innuendo and they’re using this very salacious story about Jensen Huang and this mistress and they’re trying to effectively accuse Donald Trump of doing what Joe Biden did for four years,” he continued.

Vance is referring to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang who was accused earlier this month of having an affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang. U.S. officials concluded that she was passing information to Beijing, but China has denied that she is a spy.

Jensen Huang resigned last Thursday as backlash grew, days after admitting he had an extramarital affair.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions about the scandal over why Megaspeed – the company Alice Huang worked for – was not blacklisted due to suspicions it was helping China evade chip export controls.

Trump is still supportive of Jensen Huang and pushed for the former CEO to return to his position at Nvidia though the company is reportedly not considering this idea.

“I would not mind. I would not mind that,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Asia. “I think he learned a big lesson…I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”

The president also disputed reports that Rubio warned him about Alice Huang being a spy, saying, “I haven’t heard that he said. No, I don’t know that she is a spy.”

“Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy. I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t,” Trump continued.

Trump is expected to meet with Chinese leaders while in Asia to discuss AI, national security and trade. Huang has previously accompanied Trump to Beijing in May but is no longer traveling with the president.

articles.title: Senate GOP unveils nearly $1.1T defense appropriations bill
articles.summary: Senate Republicans on Monday unveiled a nearly $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill for fiscal year 2027, which includes tens of billions in funding for programs initially part of the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation request The massive spending bill saw close to $69 billion being moved from reconciliation to the base budget, reflecting the skepticism that…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans on Monday unveiled a nearly $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill for fiscal year 2027, which includes tens of billions in funding for programs initially part of the Pentagon’s $350 billion reconciliation request

The massive spending bill saw close to $69 billion being moved from reconciliation to the base budget, reflecting the skepticism that the full $350 billion party-line Pentagon request could materialize.

The defense bill, rolled out by the Senate Appropriations Committee Republicans, features $202.9 billion for the pay and benefits of service members and families to fund a 3.6 percent pay raise $47.2 billion for munitions procurement and acceleration investments across the Pentagon and $35.6 billion for investments in air and missile defense capabilities, including the Golden Dome, a priority for President Trump.

The legislation, which does not include military construction, contains $11.1 billion for procurement of aircraft, modifications and sustainment, $6.2 billion for continued research, development and procurement of drone and counter-drone systems and $42 billion for shipbuilding, which includes nearly $2 billion in additional funding for an Arleigh Burke-class Navy guided-missile destroyer.

The bill’s release comes as lawmakers are staring down a Dec. 11 deadline to avert a government shutdown. Some Democrats are looking at the looming deadline as an opportunity to force the Trump administration to end the war against Iran, potentially throwing a curveball into the lame-duck session.

Over $285 billion in the bill is designated for procurement of weapon systems and $203 billion for research, development and testing of platforms.

The bill also contains $5.4 billion to strengthen security cooperation programs, including about $1 billion for the First Island Chain Security Cooperation Initiative to bolster partnerships with the Philippines and Taiwan, $750 million for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, some $175 million for the Baltic Security Initiative and upped funding for security cooperation with Jordan and Bahrain.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), the chairman of the Senate Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, said the bill is a “roadmap to sustainably and responsibly” deliver “generational investments” in the national defense.

“The nature of warfare is changing, and America’s adversaries are working together to threaten us. Deterring these threats is a project bigger than one-time surges of cash. From expanding critical munitions production to reviving American shipbuilding to holding our edge in developing future weapons, tomorrow’s joint force will need consistent investment, year after year,” McConnell said in a statement .

“I’m proud of the Subcommittee’s work toward an historic new baseline and a full-year investment in this generational project,” he added.

Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have advocated for a record $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget, arguing it is necessary to strengthen the military, bolster national security and revitalize the defense industrial base.

Last week, the president once again called on the Senate to pass the $350 billion partisan reconciliation package

But Democrats have been opposed to the $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget ask, and some have argued the topline for the base budget needs to be shaved off.

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, said the defense bill delivers a “truly massive windfall” for Hegseth’s Pentagon, ”meeting President Trump’s eye-popping request—while doing next to nothing to rein in this president who is waging illegal wars.”

“We cannot and should not accept the roadmap Senate Republicans have laid out which would hurl hundreds of billions of dollars more at the Pentagon while doing exceptionally little to help families get by,” Murray said in a statement on Monday.
